title: Galois groups of Keller fibers
W: Gallagher (2026) built, for every n>=3, a polynomial map C^3->C^3 with constant nonzero Jacobian whose general fibre has exactly n points. Determine the symmetry (monodromy/Galois) group of how those n points are permuted.
M: Let $H_n:\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^3$ be Gallagher's Keller map of geometric degree $n$ (A. Gallagher, \emph{An infinite family of counterexamples to the Jacobian Conjecture in dimension three}, Zenodo 2026, doi:10.5281/zenodo.21479195), so $[\mathbb C(x,y,z):H_n^*\mathbb C(X,Y,Z)]=n$. For each $n\ge3$ determine the Galois group of the Galois closure of $\mathbb C(x,y,z)/H_n^*\mathbb C(X,Y,Z)$ (equivalently the monodromy group of the $n$-sheeted covering over a general point), as a permutation group of degree $n$; and the arithmetic group over $\mathbb Q$.
why: The monodromy group is the first invariant distinguishing Keller counterexamples beyond fibre size; e.g. it decides whether inverse branches are expressible by radicals and separates families up to polynomial equivalence. Companion papers already compute it (S_n, A_n, wreath products) for other 2026 Keller families.
issues: Original M did not cite or define the family; fixed with reference and a definite object (permutation group, geometric and arithmetic). Closely analogous computations are already done: Kistner-Shaska get A_N/S_N for cyclic and beta-Hermite graded Keller families, Shaska gets S_3 for the degree-3 map, and a marked-root paper gets wreath products. Gallagher's fibres come from a tangency polynomial; the expected answer (S_n, possibly A_n) likely follows by a routine discriminant/Morse-specialization argument, so low depth. Could not open the Zenodo preprint (access blocked), so the exact formula was not checked.

title: Charge on a Fermat conductor
W: Put a unit of electric charge on a perfectly conducting solid x^4+y^4+z^4 <= 1. Show that the surface charge is thinnest exactly at the six flat points (+-1,0,0),... and thickest exactly at the eight points in the diagonal directions.
M: Let $K=\{x^4+y^4+z^4\le1\}\subset\mathbb R^3$ and let $\mu=\rho\,d\sigma$ be its Newtonian (capacitary) equilibrium measure, $\sigma$ surface measure on $\partial K$ ($\rho$ is real-analytic and positive since $\partial K$ is analytic). Prove that $\min_{\partial K}\rho$ is attained exactly at $(\pm1,0,0),(0,\pm1,0),(0,0,\pm1)$ and $\max_{\partial K}\rho$ exactly at $3^{-1/4}(\pm1,\pm1,\pm1)$.
why: It is folklore that charge accumulates where a conductor is more curved, but the density is nonlocal and only exactly known for ellipsoids (where it is proportional to K^{1/4}). The Fermat superball is the simplest smooth convex body that is not an ellipsoid and has flat points; here Gaussian curvature K=9x^2y^2z^2/(x^6+y^6+z^6)^2 even vanishes along three whole great curves, so rho cannot be a function of K, and a proof needs a genuinely nonlocal comparison argument.
issues: Statement is well posed. Quick boundary-element check (8112 panels): rho about 0.0378 at flat points, 0.062 at (2^{-1/4},2^{-1/4},0), 0.087 at the diagonal, decreasing monotonically away from the diagonal, so the conjecture is numerically consistent (a spurious max came from badly shaped mesh cells near the cube-sphere corners). No literature found on extremal points of equilibrium density for superballs. Special-instance flavour keeps it out of A.

title: Multiplicities on the Fermat quartic
W: The surface x^4+y^4+z^4 = 1 has exactly the 48 symmetries of a cube. Show its Laplace eigenvalues repeat no more often than those symmetries force (at most 3 times), except possibly for finitely many eigenvalues.
M: Let $S=\{x^4+y^4+z^4=1\}\subset\mathbb R^3$ with the induced metric (isometry group the hyperoctahedral group of order 48, whose irreducible representations have dimension $\le3$). Prove that all but finitely many eigenvalues of $\Delta_S$ have multiplicity $\le3$.
why: Uhlenbeck and Zelditch-type genericity results say that for a generic G-invariant metric every eigenspace is an irreducible G-module. No explicit, non-homogeneous surface is known to satisfy this, so proving it for one concrete algebraic surface would be a real step.
issues: Faithful, well posed. But it is one arbitrary instance of a genericity statement that is out of reach for every explicit surface; even simplicity of infinitely many eigenvalues for a single explicit asymmetric metric is open. Nothing makes the Fermat quartic special, and no method is in sight. Gimmicky choice of instance.

title: Codes avoiding square distances
W: Find the largest set of binary strings of length n in which no two differ in a perfect-square number of positions. Does it grow exponentially in n, and if so at what rate? This is a hypercube version of Sarkozy's theorem on square differences.
M: Let $A(n)=\max\{|C|: C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,\ d_H(x,y)\notin\{1,4,9,16,\dots\}\ \forall x\ne y\in C\}$. Decide whether $A(n)=2^{o(n)}$. More precisely, determine $\liminf_n\frac1n\log_2A(n)$ and $\limsup_n\frac1n\log_2A(n)$ (in particular whether they are equal).
why: It is a Sarkozy-Furstenberg question (sets with no square difference) moved to the Hamming cube, sitting between Frankl-Rodl (forbid one distance, giving (2-delta)^n) and Frankl-Wilson-type modular bounds (forbidding residue classes gives polynomial size). Squares avoid no residue class yet are sparse, so neither tool settles it, and the answer decides whether exponential codes must realize square distances.
issues: Original asked for lim, whose existence is unclear (concatenation does not preserve square-freeness of distances), so it was replaced with liminf/limsup plus the yes/no core. Attack: Frankl-Rodl with an even square in [eps n,(1-eps)n] gives a rate below 1. Natural constructions fail: product codes give subset sums of distances, which hit squares; mod-4 codes (distances 2,3 mod 4) reduce to Oddtown/Frankl-Wilson and have polynomial size; codes with all distances between two consecutive squares are near-equidistant and polynomial by Alon's rank lemma. So the rate might be 0, and it is open either way. Exact small values computed: A(1..7)=1,2,4,5,10,12,14. No literature found on infinite forbidden sets such as the squares; recent work covers single distances and arithmetic progressions (Dong-Gao-Liu-Ouyang-Zhou).

title: Square-sum cliques
W: How many distinct positive integers can have every pairwise sum a perfect square? Five are known (Nicolas 1971); six is unknown. Decide whether the size is bounded.
M: Let $s=\sup\{|X|: X\subset\mathbb Z_{>0}\text{ finite},\ a+b\in\{k^2\}\ \forall a\ne b\in X\}$. Decide whether $s<\infty$ (the first open case: does a 6-element set exist?).
why: A classical Diophantine problem in the line of Diophantine m-tuples. The k-element sets are integral points on varieties that become of general type as k grows, so conjectures of Bombieri-Lang type predict a bound, but no unconditional bound is known.
issues: M referred to an undefined $\omega(S_N)$; rewritten to be self-contained. Not novel: an old, well-known problem (Thatcher, Math. Gazette 1978; Prime Puzzles Problem 70; the largest known set is 5, {7442, 28658, 148583, 177458, 763442}). Valuable but known, so it does not belong on a novel-problems list unless the list is labelled as classic.

title: Chaos in the double pendulum at every energy
W: The planar double pendulum with equal masses and equal arms looks chaotic at moderate energies but almost regular at very low and very high energies. Prove that it has genuine (positive-entropy) chaos at every energy above the rest state.
M: Let $H(\theta_1,\theta_2,p_1,p_2)$ be the Hamiltonian of the planar double pendulum with $m_1=m_2=\ell_1=\ell_2=g=1$ on $T^*\mathbb T^2$, with minimum value $E_0$ (the hanging rest state). Prove that for every $E>E_0$ the Hamiltonian flow restricted to $\{H=E\}$ has positive topological entropy.
why: The double pendulum is the standard textbook example of chaos, yet rigorous chaos is not known uniformly in energy. Both ends are near-integrable: at low energy it is a nonresonant pair of oscillators (frequency ratio 1+sqrt2), and at high energy it is nearly free rotation. Chaos there needs exponentially small splitting estimates, and the middle range needs computer-assisted proofs, so it is a concrete test for both techniques.
issues: M was essentially correct; clarified the phase space. Main attack: the low-energy limit is linear and integrable (numerics show the chaotic fraction tends to 0 as E tends to E_0, arXiv 2312.13436), so positive entropy must come from exponentially thin stochastic layers near resonances. Note the high-energy end is also near-integrable, which W originally ignored. I found no rigorous positive-entropy result at any energy (web search budget ran out before I could confirm non-integrability references such as Morales-Ramis-type results). Natural but technical, so B rather than A.

title: Capacities of the 4D superball
W: Viterbo's conjecture that all symplectic capacities agree on convex bodies is false in general, but the known counterexample is not centrally symmetric. On the 4D ball x1^4+y1^4+x2^4+y2^4 <= 1 the cylindrical and Ekeland-Hofer-Zehnder capacities are both known to equal 4Gamma(5/4)^2/Gamma(3/2). Does the largest symplectically embedded round ball have the same capacity?
M: Let $U=\{x_1^4+y_1^4+x_2^4+y_2^4\le1\}\subset(\mathbb R^4,dx_1\wedge dy_1+dx_2\wedge dy_2)$. It is known that $c_{EHZ}(U)=c_Z(U)=c_0:=4\Gamma(5/4)^2/\Gamma(3/2)\approx3.708$. Decide whether the Gromov width $c_G(U)=\sup\{\pi r^2: B^4(r)\hookrightarrow U\text{ symplectically}\}$ equals $c_0$.
why: After Haim-Kislev and Ostrover disproved Viterbo's conjecture, it is open whether all normalized capacities still agree on centrally symmetric convex bodies. The l^4 ball is the simplest centrally symmetric, non-toric convex body whose EHZ and cylindrical capacities are known exactly, so its Gromov width is the sharpest remaining test: a strict inequality would give a centrally symmetric counterexample to strong Viterbo.
issues: Original M asked whether c_G = c_EHZ without noting that c_EHZ(U) = c_Z(U) was computed in 2026 (arXiv 2609.37794, Theorem 2, p=4). The problem therefore reduces to the Gromov width alone, and M was rewritten that way. Trivial bound: U contains the Euclidean unit ball, so c_G >= pi. U is not toric, so ECH and toric methods do not apply directly. No Gromov-width computation for l^p balls found (search budget exhausted before a dedicated search).

title: Sofa stability
W: Baek (2024) proved that Gerver's sofa has the largest area among shapes that can be moved around a right-angled corner in a hallway of width 1. Show that any movable sofa whose area is nearly Gerver's must be nearly Gerver's sofa in shape (which in particular gives uniqueness).
M: A moving sofa is a compact connected $S\subset\mathbb R^2$ that can be moved by a continuous rigid motion from $(-\infty,0]\times[0,1]$ to $[0,1]\times(-\infty,0]$ inside $L=((-\infty,1]\times[0,1])\cup([0,1]\times(-\infty,1])$. Let $G$ be Gerver's sofa, of area $A_G\approx2.21953$. Prove that there are $C,\alpha>0$ such that every moving sofa $S$ with $|S|\ge A_G-\varepsilon$ satisfies $\min_{g}|gS\,\triangle\,G|\le C\varepsilon^{\alpha}$, the minimum over rigid motions $g$ of the plane.
why: Baek's proof gives optimality, but its abstract claims neither uniqueness nor stability. A quantitative stability inequality is the standard sharpening of an isoperimetric-type theorem, as for Bonnesen-type and Fusco-Maggi-Pratelli results, and would make the solution robust, for example for numerical verification.
issues: Original used Hausdorff distance, which is not controlled by area (zero-area appendages could change it), so it was switched to symmetric-difference area. Also defined the hallway and the class of sofas, and made C, alpha existential. Even qualitative uniqueness seems not to be stated in Baek's abstract, so the alpha-free version is already open. Technical follow-up, B.

title: Prime Markov triples
W: Markov triples are positive integer solutions of x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz. Are there infinitely many in which all three numbers are prime?
M: Decide whether infinitely many solutions $(x,y,z)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^3$ of $x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz$ have $x,y,z$ all prime.
why: It combines the Markov tree, which governs the worst-approximable numbers and the Lagrange spectrum, with primality of sparse, doubly exponentially growing sequences, in the same spirit as the open question of infinitely many prime Markov numbers.
issues: Well posed but likely hopeless and heuristically settled. Search of the 3502 smallest triples (entries below 10^60) finds exactly 5 all-prime triples: (2,5,29), (5,29,433), (2,5741,33461), (5,2897,43261), and one with min 89 and two 22-25 digit entries. Prime-number heuristics give a convergent expected count: about the sum over the tree of 1/(log x log y log z), which behaves like a sum of 1/(ab(a+b)) over a 2-dimensional set of log-sizes. Fixed-small-entry branches (e.g. x=2, the odd Pell numbers) need twin-prime indices and also converge. So the expected answer is 'finitely many', and that is unprovable with current methods; no structure makes it attractive.

title: Quintic Szego growth
W: The cubic Szego equation on the circle is completely integrable, and Gerard-Grellier showed that its smooth solutions can have Sobolev norms that are unbounded in time. Decide whether the quintic Szego equation, which is presumably not integrable, also has smooth solutions with unbounded high Sobolev norms.
M: On $L^2_+(\mathbb T)=\{u\in L^2:\hat u(k)=0\ \forall k<0\}$ with Szego projector $\Pi$, consider $i\partial_tu=\Pi(|u|^4u)$, which is globally well posed in $H^s_+$, $s>1/2$, with conserved $\|u\|_{L^2}$, $(Du,u)$ and $\|u\|_{L^6}$. Decide whether there exist $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb T)\cap L^2_+$ and $s>1/2$ with $\limsup_{t\to\infty}\|u(t)\|_{H^s}=\infty$.
why: Unbounded Sobolev growth (weak turbulence) is proven almost only for integrable models such as cubic Szego, using their Lax pairs. The quintic Szego equation keeps the same conservation laws and the H^{1/2} bound but loses integrability, so it is a clean model for asking whether turbulent cascades survive without integrable structure, in the spirit of Bourgain's question for NLS.
issues: Statement is well posed after recording the conservation laws and global well-posedness (H^{1/2} conservation plus a Brezis-Gallouet argument, as in the cubic case; worth double-checking). Literature check incomplete: web search budget ran out before I could search for prior work on quintic or higher-power Szego equations, so novelty is uncertain and needs a check. Hard and natural, but likely out of reach as stated.

title: Knotted billiards in a regular tetrahedron
W: A billiard ball bouncing periodically inside a regular tetrahedron, without hitting edges or corners, traces a closed polygon in space. Is any such polygon knotted, and do infinitely many different knot types occur?
M: Call a periodic billiard trajectory in a regular tetrahedron $T\subset\mathbb R^3$ admissible if it never meets an edge or vertex of $T$ and its image is an embedded closed polygon. (a) Does some admissible trajectory form a nontrivial knot? (b) Prove that the set of knot types of admissible periodic trajectories is infinite.
why: In the cube, periodic billiard trajectories are exactly the Lissajous knots (Jones-Przytycki), and infinitely many knot types occur because the cube unfolds to a lattice. The regular tetrahedron does not tile space and its dihedral angle arccos(1/3) is an irrational multiple of pi, so its unfolding group is not discrete. Even the existence of periodic orbits in tetrahedra is subtle, and knot types are an untouched invariant here.
issues: Added part (a), because even one knotted orbit is not obviously known. A trajectory may traverse its image twice (odd periods), so the knot type is defined from the image. I did not do a numerical periodic-orbit search. Literature check incomplete (search budget exhausted); possible prior work on billiard knots in polyhedra other than the cube and cylinder should be checked.

title: Integer-bijective Keller map
W: Find a polynomial map with integer coefficients and Jacobian 1 that permutes the integer points but has no polynomial inverse.
M: Find $F\in\mathbb{Z}[x_1,\dots,x_n]^n$ with $\det DF\equiv 1$ such that $F|_{\mathbb{Z}^n}$ is a bijection of $\mathbb{Z}^n$ but $F$ is not a polynomial automorphism.
why: Any such map would be a counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture with an extra arithmetic property, so the question is at least as hard as disproving the Jacobian conjecture.
issues: Trivialisation (sketch, answer = no such F exists). (1) Bijective on Z^n implies F mod p is surjective, hence bijective, on F_p^n for every p, because every residue class contains an integer value. (2) A Keller map has generic degree d=[C(x):C(F)]. If d>=2, take a dense open U over which F is finite etale. Its geometric monodromy group is transitive of degree d, and by Jordan's lemma it contains a derangement. For the positive-density set of primes that split completely in the constant field of the Galois closure, Chebotarev/Lang-Weil gives about c p^n points y in U(F_p) whose Frobenius is a derangement. Such y have no F_p-preimage, which contradicts surjectivity mod p. (3) So d=1, F is birational, and Keller's 1939 theorem says a birational Keller map is an automorphism. Also, the inverse lies automatically in Z[x] when det DF=1, so 'automorphism over Z' and 'over C' agree. The object cannot exist. Surjectivity of F on Z^n already suffices. This is a routine argument (not checked line by line, but standard Fried-Jarden-style). Literature: arXiv 1712.02113 has related integral-point reformulations of JC.

title: Closed-form Euler blow-up
W: Smooth compactly supported starting data for the 3D Euler equations that blow up in finite time are now known to exist, but the construction is an infinite iterative series. Give such data as an explicit formula.
M: Find an explicit divergence-free $u_0=\nabla\times\big(P(x)e^{-|x|^2}\big)$ with $P\in\mathbb{Q}[x_1,x_2,x_3]^3$ (or another explicitly specified finite closed-form class) such that the unforced 3D incompressible Euler solution on $\mathbb{R}^3$ with $u(0)=u_0$ has finite maximal smooth lifespan.
why: An explicit blow-up datum would let the singularity be checked numerically and studied concretely, beyond pure existence. It is a refinement of the now-resolved existence question.
issues: The core question (smooth, finite-energy, unforced Euler blow-up on R^3) appears to be resolved in 2026: OpenAI 'Finite Time Blowup for the Euler Equation' (smooth compactly supported data, Lean-formalised) and Fan Zheng's exposition arXiv 2610.02509. That construction gives data as a limit of an iterative series, not in closed form. 'Closed-form' was undefined, so I fixed it to an explicit finite class. The residual question is fairly arbitrary. Not elite.

title: Non-arithmetic tones of the cube
W: Many vibration frequencies of a cube's surface come from flat tori and are rational multiples of pi squared. Prove that at least one frequency is not of this form.
M: Let $S$ be the boundary of the unit cube $[0,1]^3$ with its intrinsic flat metric (8 cone points of angle $3\pi/2$), and let $\Delta$ be the Friedrichs extension of the Laplacian on $S$. Prove that some eigenvalue of $\Delta$ is not in $\pi^2\mathbb{Q}$.
why: Flat cone surfaces whose cone angles are not of the form 2pi/k cannot be quotients of tori. Numerics show 'singular' eigenfunctions, non-smooth at the vertices, with eigenvalues that look non-arithmetic. Proving that even one of them is non-arithmetic would separate diffractive spectral geometry from lattice-arithmetic behaviour, in the simplest Platonic example.
issues: Numerical work (arXiv 1809.09909) splits cube eigenfunctions into nonsingular (torus-type) and singular ones, e.g. lambda_38 approx 8.06, with most of the spectrum singular. I found no proof of non-arithmeticity. Trace-formula and Weyl-law arguments do not obviously exclude a spectrum inside pi^2 Q with unbounded denominators, so this is genuinely transcendence-flavoured. I fixed M to specify the metric and the self-adjoint extension. Narrow but clean.

title: Sharp linear firefighter constant on Z^3
W: On the 3D grid, any finite fire can be contained if the number of firefighters you place grows linearly in time, and sublinear growth fails. Find the exact critical slope.
M: Firefighter game on $\mathbb{Z}^3$ (nearest-neighbour graph): a finite set $X_0$ burns at time 0. At each step $t=1,2,\dots$ one first protects $\lfloor ct\rfloor$ unburnt vertices (permanently), then fire spreads to all unprotected neighbours of burning vertices. Let $c^*=\inf\{c>0:\text{for every finite }X_0\text{ the fire can be contained}\}$. Determine $c^*$, or at least prove $0<c^*<\infty$ with explicit bounds.
why: Develin and Hartke showed that no constant number of firefighters suffices on Z^d for d>=3. Later work established that order t^{d-2} firefighters per step is exactly the right growth rate, which is linear for Z^3. The sharp constant is the natural next question and is tied to discrete isoperimetry of fire fronts.
issues: The original M was ill-posed. From a single vertex, 5 firefighters per step already suffice on Z^3 (Wang-Moeller, with 2d-1 sharp by Develin-Hartke), so the original f(t)/t tends to 0. The right formulation quantifies over all finite outbreaks with rate ct; I rewrote M that way. Known: O(n^{d-2}) suffices (Dyer-Martinez-Pedroza-Thorne), and o(n^{d-2}) fails for polynomial-growth Cayley graphs (arXiv 2002.11205). I found no work on the constant. A scaling heuristic suggests c* is in (0,infinity), but positivity of c* may itself need proof.

title: Square-sum coloring
W: Join two different numbers if they add up to a perfect square. Does the number of colours needed stay bounded?
M: Let $S_N$ have vertex set $\{1,\dots,N\}$ with $x\sim y$ iff $x\neq y$ and $x+y$ is a square. Decide whether $\sup_N\chi(S_N)<\infty$.
why: This is a classical partition-regularity question for x+y=z^2.
issues: Known: the answer is no, the chromatic number is unbounded. Khalfalah-Szemeredi (CPC 2006) proved that every finite colouring of N has x and y of the same colour, x not equal to y, with x+y a perfect square. Distinctness is needed for the result to have content, since x=y=2m^2 is trivial. So the infinite graph has infinite chromatic number, and by de Bruijn-Erdos compactness sup_N chi(S_N) is infinite. Related work: Green-Lindqvist (arXiv 1608.08374), Pach (arXiv 1805.06279).

title: Chaos in the symmetric ABC flow
W: The ABC flow with all three coefficients equal to 1 is the classical steady Euler flow on the 3-torus that is believed to be chaotic. Prove that it really is: show it has positive topological entropy.
M: Prove that the flow of $\dot x=\sin z+\cos y,\ \dot y=\sin x+\cos z,\ \dot z=\sin y+\cos x$ on $\mathbb{T}^3=(\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z})^3$ has positive topological entropy (e.g. by exhibiting a transversal homoclinic orbit to a hyperbolic periodic orbit, or a horseshoe for a Poincare map).
why: The 1:1:1 ABC flow is the standard example of Lagrangian chaos in a steady Beltrami (Euler) flow, and of fast-dynamo and mixing studies since Arnold and Henon. The numerical evidence for chaos since Dombre et al. (1986) is overwhelming, yet only non-integrability (Ziglin) and existence of particular periodic or ballistic orbits are proved. A proof, likely computer-assisted, would close a forty-year gap.
issues: Literature: Ziglin proved analytic non-integrability for A=B=C. Xin-Yu-Zlatos (arXiv 1601.02724) proved existence of periodic orbits. Lessard et al. (arXiv 1704.03128) gave computer-assisted proofs of ballistic orbits and stated that further ABC work was planned. A 2026 paper (arXiv 2609.17449) gives C^1 non-integrability only in a small-parameter regime. I found no proof of positive entropy or a horseshoe at A=B=C=1. The statement is clean and the system matches the standard ABC form. It is likely tractable by CAPD-style validated numerics, which lowers 'depth' but not interest.

title: Cross-polytopes in 4D
W: Every smooth convex body in 4-space should have the eight corners of a regular cross-polytope lying on its boundary.
M: Prove that for every smooth convex body $K\subset\mathbb{R}^4$ there is a regular cross-polytope (a similar copy of $\mathrm{conv}\{\pm e_1,\dots,\pm e_4\}$) all of whose 8 vertices lie on $\partial K$.
why: Inscribing regular octahedra and cross-polytopes (Klee-Wagon Problem 11.5) is a high-dimensional cousin of the square peg problem. Karasev settled every odd prime power dimension with equivariant topology, but the method fails in even dimensions. Dimension 4 is the first open case and needs a genuinely new obstruction computation.
issues: Makeev solved d=3 for smooth bodies, and Karasev (arXiv 0905.2671) solved odd prime powers d for non-angular bodies, noting the method does not apply to d=2. Centrally symmetric bodies are handled in all d via Yamabe-Yujobo. Akopyan-Karasev handle polytopes in R^3. I found no result for d=4. I restricted M to smooth bodies: for arbitrary convex bodies, limiting arguments can degenerate, and Karasev notes that even dropping non-angularity is unclear. Already posed implicitly, so novelty is low.

title: Superlinear unit distances on the unit sphere
W: In 2026 a number-field construction showed that points in the plane can have n^(1+c) unit distances, disproving Erdos's conjecture. On a sphere of radius 1/sqrt2 an n^(4/3) construction is classical, but on the unit sphere only n·sqrt(log n) is known. Can the new ideas give a power gain there?
M: Prove or disprove: there is $c>0$ such that for infinitely many $n$ there exist $P\subset S^2=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^3:|x|=1\}$ with $|P|=n$ and $\#\{\{p,q\}\subset P:|p-q|=1\}\ge n^{1+c}$.
why: On S^2, distance 1 means angle 60 degrees, an inhomogeneous condition that lattice constructions only give n^(1+o(1)) for. The orthogonality trick that gives n^{4/3} at radius 1/sqrt2 has no analogue. A power gain would show the 2026 planar phenomenon is robust, while a matching n^{1+o(1)} upper bound would show the sphere behaves like the conjectured old plane.
issues: Known: radius 1/sqrt2 gives Theta(n^{4/3}) (Erdos-Hickerson-Pach), any radius has upper bound O(n^{4/3}), and general radius >1/2 has lower bound Omega(n sqrt(log n)) (Swanepoel-Valtr 2004). The question of power gains for other radii goes back to EHP, so it is not novel. The 2026 planar disproof (OpenAI; Sawin arXiv 2605.20579 with n^{1.014}; Alon et al. remarks arXiv 2605.20695) treats only the plane, and Sawin notes serious obstacles in R^3. My quick lattice heuristic (directions v/|v| with |v|^2 in s·squares) gives only linear counts. M is unchanged apart from 'prove or disprove'.

title: Burgers with degenerate critical dissipation
W: Critical half-Laplacian dissipation keeps Burgers smooth. Let that dissipation switch off quadratically at one point of the circle. Do shocks form there?
M: Let $a(x)=1-\cos x$ and consider $u_t+uu_x+\Lambda^{1/2}\big(a\,\Lambda^{1/2}u\big)=0$ on $\mathbb{T}$, $\Lambda=(-\partial_x^2)^{1/2}$. Decide whether every real $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb{T})$ yields a global smooth solution.
why: The question tests whether the Kiselev-Nazarov-Shterenberg regularity mechanism for critical Burgers survives a degenerate, spatially varying coefficient.
issues: Likely routine, with expected answer no. The equation preserves odd symmetry (a is even), so odd data with u_0'(0)<0 steepen at the stationary point x=0. Writing the operator as a·Lambda + [Lambda^{1/2},a]Lambda^{1/2}, the commutator is order 0. At the Burgers self-similar scale (x ~ (T-t)^{3/2}, u ~ (T-t)^{1/2}), both dissipative pieces are lower order than u_t. So stable Burgers shock formation (Buckmaster-Shkoller-Vicol style modulation, or Dong-Du-Li type arguments) should go through. Novel but narrow and probably expert-routine. Added 'real' to the data.

title: Riesz-transform Schrodinger equation
W: Couple a 2D Schrodinger wave to the Riesz transform of its own density. Mass is conserved, but there is no energy. Do smooth solutions live forever?
M: Consider $iu_t+\Delta u=u\,R_1(|u|^2)$ on $\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^2$, $\widehat{R_1f}(\xi)=-i\frac{\xi_1}{|\xi|}\hat f(\xi)$. Decide whether every $u_0\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^2)$ gives a global solution in $C(\mathbb{R},H^1)$.
why: This is a toy L^2-critical model whose real potential R_1(|u|^2) has an odd kernel. It keeps mass conservation but destroys the Hamiltonian structure, so energy and virial methods are unavailable.
issues: Checks: R_1 maps real functions to real ones, so the potential is real and mass is conserved. The kernel is odd, so the equation is not Hamiltonian, and momentum is not conserved either (the symbol xi_1 xi_j/|xi| is even and nonzero). The equation has cubic NLS scaling in 2D, so it is L^2-critical. Strichartz plus L^p-boundedness of R_1 gives L^2 local well-posedness and global existence for small mass. Large data look hard but the model is arbitrary, and I found no literature. Not elite.

title: Period-doubling torus bundles
W: Build a once-punctured torus bundle by reading the period-doubling word as a product of the two basic shear matrices. Show its hyperbolic volume per letter settles to a limit as the word grows.
M: Let $W_n\in\{a,b\}^{2^n}$ be the length-$2^n$ prefix of the fixed point of $a\mapsto ab,\ b\mapsto aa$ ($n\ge1$). Let $\phi_n\in SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ be the product obtained from $W_n$ via $a\mapsto R=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, $b\mapsto L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, and let $M_n$ be the once-punctured torus bundle with monodromy $\phi_n$ (hyperbolic since $W_n$ contains both letters). Prove that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathrm{vol}(M_n)/2^n$ exists.
why: This asks for a volume 'law of large numbers' along a deterministic, uniquely ergodic substitution sequence, the analogue of Viaggi's theorem for random mapping tori.
issues: Likely routine. For period doubling, W_{n+1}=W_nW_n with the last letter changed, so phi_{n+1}=phi_n^2·h with h in a fixed finite set. vol(phi^2)=2 vol(phi) exactly. If vol(M_{psi h}) - vol(M_psi) is bounded for bounded h, which should follow from the locality of Gueritaud's canonical layered triangulation and angle-structure maximisation (or from model-manifold almost-additivity as in Viaggi), then vol(M_n)/2^n is Cauchy with O(2^{-n}) error. The choice of period-doubling word is arbitrary. The general statement (any uniquely ergodic subshift) would be the better form but is probably also accessible.

title: Singularities of the permanental hypersurface
W: The hypersurface where the n x n determinant vanishes has rational singularities, the mildest kind that matters for much of its geometry. Decide whether the hypersurface where the n x n permanent vanishes has rational singularities for every n, and compute its minimal exponent, a finer measure of how mild a singularity is.
M: Let $X_n=\{\operatorname{per}_n=0\}\subset\mathbb A^{n^2}_{\mathbb C}$ and let $\tilde\alpha(X_n)$ be Saito's minimal exponent (the smallest root of $b_{\operatorname{per}_n}(-s)/(1-s)$), so that $\operatorname{lct}(\mathbb A^{n^2},X_n)=\min\{1,\tilde\alpha(X_n)\}$ and $X_n$ has rational singularities iff $\tilde\alpha(X_n)>1$. For $n=2$, $X_2$ is a nondegenerate quadric cone in $\mathbb A^4$ and $\tilde\alpha=2$. For $\det_n$ the Bernstein--Sato polynomial is $\prod_{i=1}^n(s+i)$, so $\tilde\alpha(\{\det_n=0\})=2$ for all $n$. Determine $\tilde\alpha(X_n)$ for all $n\ge3$ (in particular for $n=3$), and decide whether $X_n$ has rational singularities for every $n$.
why: Determinantal varieties are the model case of a well-understood singular variety; permanental varieties, which are central in algebraic complexity (Valiant's VP vs VNP, geometric complexity theory), have almost no geometric results. The minimal exponent is a single number that would quantify how differently the two polynomials behave geometrically.
issues: No literature found computing lct, b-function, minimal exponent or rationality for per_n (n>=3); 2402.17839 says geometric results on permanental varieties are essentially absent and only bounds on the codimension of the singular locus are known (von zur Gathen 1987, improved there). Fix: asking for lct is redundant, since lct = min(1, minimal exponent) and lct is 1 whenever the singularities are rational; reframed around the minimal exponent and rationality, and added the det_n benchmark. A large codimension of Sing(X_n) does not by itself imply rational singularities, so the question is not trivial, but it is fairly narrow. The case n=3 (a cubic in 9 variables) should be within reach of computer algebra.

title: Distinct character degrees of the symmetric group
W: Conjugate partitions always give representations of S_n of the same dimension, so at most about half of the p(n) irreducible representations can have distinct dimensions. Decide whether the fraction of distinct dimensions tends to a limit, and whether that limit is positive.
M: Let $d(n)=\#\{f^\lambda:\lambda\vdash n\}$ be the number of distinct irreducible character degrees of $S_n$, so $d(n)\le (p(n)+sc(n))/2$, where $sc(n)$ is the number of self-conjugate partitions. Determine whether $\lim_{n\to\infty}d(n)/p(n)$ exists and, if so, find it; in particular decide whether $\liminf_n d(n)/p(n)>0$. (Hook-length data: $d(n)/p(n)\in[0.40,0.47]$ for $20\le n\le45$, e.g. $d(40)=16216$, $p(40)=37338$; computations up to $n=129$ in arXiv:2410.01726 show the average multiplicity $p(n)/d(n)$ with no clear limit, possibly near $2.5$.)
why: Degrees of S_n are products of hook lengths, and coincidences between them beyond conjugation are a basic but poorly understood arithmetic phenomenon. Whether the average degree multiplicity stays bounded says how much of the information in a partition is lost in its dimension.
issues: Already posed in essence: arXiv:2410.01726 (On the irreducible character degrees of symmetric groups and their multiplicities) plots p(n)/|cd(S_n)| for n<=129, says it is far from clear whether a limit exists (maybe about 2.5), and records a referee's suggestion of pi*sqrt(2/3)~2.565. Not novel, but still open. Statement fine; added the upper bound with self-conjugate partitions and the reference data. The given data is consistent with the paper.

title: The complex of planar graphs
W: Planar graphs on n labelled vertices form a simplicial complex, because deleting an edge keeps a graph planar. It is pure, since every maximal planar graph has 3n-6 edges. Its homology turns out not to be that of a wedge of top-dimensional spheres: already for n=6 it is concentrated two degrees lower and has 2-torsion. Determine its homology.
M: Let $\Pi_n$ be the simplicial complex on vertex set $E(K_n)$ whose faces are edge sets of planar graphs; it is pure of dimension $3n-7$. Determine $\tilde H_*(\Pi_n;\mathbb Z)$, or at least $\tilde H_*(\Pi_n;\mathbb Q)$, for all $n$. Known: $\Pi_4$ is a simplex, $\Pi_5=\partial\Delta^9\cong S^8$. For $n=6$ (computed exactly): $\tilde H_*(\Pi_6;\mathbb Q)$ is $\mathbb Q^{15}$ in degree $9=3n-9$ and $0$ elsewhere; $\tilde H_*(\Pi_6;\mathbb F_2)$ is $\mathbb F_2^{15},\mathbb F_2,\mathbb F_2$ in degrees $9,10,11$, so $\tilde H_{10}(\Pi_6;\mathbb Z)$ has $2$-torsion and $\Pi_6$ is not a wedge of spheres. The mod-2 top class is the sum of all triangulations: every face of dimension $3n-8$ of $\Pi_6$ lies in an even number (2 or 4) of facets. Questions: (a) is $\tilde H_*(\Pi_n;\mathbb Q)$ concentrated in degree $3n-9$ for all $n\ge6$, and what is its rank and $S_n$-module structure? (b) Is $\tilde H_{3n-7}(\Pi_n;\mathbb F_2)\ne0$ for all $n\ge5$? Is all torsion 2-torsion?
why: Simplicial complexes of monotone graph properties (matchings, forests, non-connected and non-k-connected graphs) are a well-developed area, and planarity is the most natural minor-closed property not yet treated. The non-orientable, triangulation-flip-driven top class makes it differ from the wedge-of-spheres pattern typical of such complexes.
issues: ORIGINAL STATEMENT FALSE: a quick exact computation (GF(2) and rational boundary ranks over all 2^15 subgraphs of K_6) gives rational reduced homology Q^15 in degree 9 only, and mod-2 homology F2^15, F2, F2 in degrees 9, 10, 11. So Pi_6 is not a wedge of 11-spheres; the Euler characteristic -15 is correct but misleading. Rewrote M as a homology-determination problem, keeping the n=6 data. The claimed chi(Pi_7)=177 was not re-verified; it would imply rational homology in an even degree, for example 3n-9=12. No literature found on this complex. Jonsson's LNM 1928 Table 7.1 lists monotone graph properties studied, and planarity does not appear in the sources checked.

title: Alternating quotients of knot groups
W: The trefoil's group maps onto every alternating group A_n with n>=9, because modulo its centre it is the modular group. Show that every nontrivial knot group maps onto A_n for all large n, or at least for infinitely many n, and bound the last exception in terms of the knot.
M: Let $K\subset S^3$ be a nontrivial knot and $G_K=\pi_1(S^3\setminus K)$. (a) Prove that $G_K$ surjects onto $A_n$ for all $n\ge N(K)$, and bound $N(K)$ in terms of the crossing number. (b) Weaker: prove that $G_K$ surjects onto $A_n$ for infinitely many $n$, or even for one $n\ge5$. Data (exhaustive search over pairs of conjugate even permutations, meridians $x,y$ with $wx=yw$): for the trefoil ($w=xy$) a surjection exists exactly for $n=5$ and $n\ge9$, since every surjection kills the centre and factors through $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb Z)\cong C_2*C_3$, and Miller proved $(2,3)$-generation of $A_n$ for $n\ne3,6,7,8$. For the figure-eight knot ($w=x^{-1}yxy^{-1}$) a surjection exists for $n=6,9,10$ and not for $n=5,7,8$. Is $N(4_1)=9$, i.e. does $G_{4_1}$ surject onto $A_n$ for every $n\ge9$?
why: Dunfield and Thurston asked whether every finite-volume hyperbolic 3-manifold group has an alternating quotient; whether this holds for infinitely many or all large n is also open, and Fuchsian groups are known to have all large alternating quotients (Everitt, Liebeck-Shalev). Knot complements are the most concrete test case: their groups are normally generated by a meridian and are strongly constrained, and an answer would clarify what finite quotients knot groups have, which matters for profinite rigidity.
issues: Special case of open questions: Dunfield-Thurston Question 7.6 (existence of an A_n quotient for hyperbolic 3-manifolds), and Button (arXiv 1010.2726) notes it is unknown whether such manifolds have A_n quotients for infinitely many or all but finitely many n. So it is not fully novel, but the knot-group formulation with an effective N(K) does not appear in what I found. Verified by computer: the trefoil gives n=5 yes, n=6,7 no; the figure-eight gives n=5,7,8 no and n=6,9 yes. Checked the trefoil argument (the centre (xy)^3 must map trivially). Torus knots follow from Everitt's theorem on free products of cyclic groups. Added the weaker form (b), since even it appears open for hyperbolic knots.

title: Smallest-degree Keller counterexamples in dimension 3
W: In 2026 the Jacobian conjecture was shown false in dimension 3: there are polynomial maps C^3 -> C^3 with constant nonzero Jacobian that are not invertible, and the known examples have degree 7. Decide whether such a map can have degree at most 4. More generally, find the smallest degree a counterexample in dimension 3 can have.
M: Let $d_3=\min\{\deg F: F\in\mathbb C[x,y,z]^3,\ \det DF\in\mathbb C^\times,\ F\notin\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb C^3)\}$, where $\deg F=\max_i\deg F_i$. By Wang's theorem $d_3\ge3$, and the 2026 examples (Alp\"oge; van den Essen) give $d_3\le7$. Decide whether $d_3\le4$, i.e. whether every Keller map $\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^3$ of degree $\le4$ is an automorphism. Ultimately, determine $d_3$.
why: Once the Jacobian conjecture failed in dimension 3, the natural next question is where exactly it fails. The minimal degree of a counterexample tells us how far the classical positive results (Wang for degree 2, the reductions to cubic maps) can be pushed in a fixed dimension, and a degree-3 or degree-4 counterexample would bear on the cubic-homogeneous reduction.
issues: The original M asked to PROVE degree <=4 Keller maps on C^3 are automorphisms. In this period the Jacobian conjecture has been refuted in dimension 3 (Alpöge, July 2026; van den Essen's elementary version has component degrees 7,6,4; Gao/Gallagher families; Isabelle/AFP formal verification). The degree-<=4 case does not appear settled in what I found, but its truth value is now unclear, so the statement was changed from 'prove' to 'decide', with the minimal degree d_3 as the real target. Not checked: whether some of the newer families (Gallagher H_d, Gao) already reach polynomial degree <=6 or <=5; their papers mostly report geometric degree (fibre size), not polynomial degree. Whether degree-3 maps in dimension 3 are settled classically is also unverified, so d_3>=3 is the only safe lower bound.

title: Drum tones of superellipses
W: Take the region |x|^p + |y|^p <= r^p, scaled to have area 1. At p = 2 it is a disk, which has the lowest possible bass note of any region of that area (Faber–Krahn). As p grows to infinity it becomes a square, whose note is higher. Show that the note rises steadily the whole way from p = 2 to infinity.
M: For $p\in[2,\infty)$ let $D_p=\{(x,y):|x|^p+|y|^p\le r_p^p\}$ with $r_p$ chosen so that $|D_p|=1$, and let $\lambda_1(p)$ be the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of $-\Delta$ on $D_p$. Prove that $\lambda_1$ is strictly increasing on $[2,\infty)$, with $\lambda_1(2)=\pi j_{0,1}^2$ and $\lambda_1(p)\uparrow2\pi^2$ as $p\to\infty$.
why: This is a test case for how the Dirichlet eigenvalue moves along a natural one-parameter family of convex sets joining the Faber–Krahn minimiser (the disk) to the square. Monotonicity along such families is a known hard type of question in shape optimisation, since Hadamard's formula gives the derivative but not its sign.
issues: I computed it with the method of particular solutions, using a D4-symmetric Fourier–Bessel basis. The area-normalised lambda_1 comes out at 18.168 (p=2), 18.262 (2.5), 18.431 (3), 18.752 (4), 18.991 (5), 19.159 (6), 19.367 (8), 19.482 (10), 19.614 (15), 19.666 (20), 19.727 (50), heading up to 2pi^2 = 19.739. It is cleanly increasing, so the conjecture looks true, with no counterexample. I found no literature on this exact family, so it is novel but narrow. A proof via Hadamard's shape derivative would need sign information on |du/dn|^2 tested against the normal velocity of the boundary, which looks technical rather than deep. I added the endpoint values to M. The p in [1,2] side (where the shape tends to the rotated square at p=1) is a natural companion question. Knill et al.'s paper on billiards in l^p unit balls lists the Dirichlet eigenvalues of these tables as an open topic, so the family has been looked at but this monotonicity question is not posed there.

title: Irrationality of the quartic oscillator ground state
W: The lowest energy of the quartic oscillator, -d^2/dx^2 + x^4 on the line, is about 1.0603620905. Show that it is irrational.
M: Let $E_0=\min\sigma\big(-\tfrac{d^2}{dx^2}+x^4\big)$, the operator taken self-adjoint on $L^2(\mathbb R)$ ($E_0=1.06036209048418\ldots$). Prove that $E_0\notin\mathbb Q$.
why: Irrationality and transcendence are known for spectral data of exactly solvable problems, such as Bessel zeros via Siegel's theorem. For a genuinely non-solvable Schrödinger operator, apparently nothing is known. Voros's exact WKB and spectral-determinant functional relations describe E_0 implicitly, so a proof would have to turn those relations, or a series or continued fraction for E_0, into Diophantine information.
issues: The numerical value is correct. I found no literature on the arithmetic nature of E_0; it is novel in the sense of never having been posed explicitly. The statement is precise. There is no realistic route: no available tool gives irrationality of a constant defined only implicitly through a non-solvable ODE. So this is a clean 'benchmark of ignorance' rather than an attackable problem, and the specific choice of x^4 and of E_0 is somewhat arbitrary. Graded B for cleanness, kept below A because it is likely hopeless and not tied to a broader programme.

title: Graceful labellings of forests
W: A forest with m edges and c trees has m + c vertices. Label them with 0, 1, ..., m + c - 1, each label used once, so that the m edge differences |label(u) - label(v)| are all different. Show that every forest has such a labelling. The case 'a tree plus one isolated vertex' already says that every tree can be labelled gracefully if one spare label is allowed.
M: Prove that every forest $F$ with $m$ edges and $c\ge1$ components has a bijection $\ell:V(F)\to\{0,1,\dots,m+c-1\}$ such that the values $|\ell(u)-\ell(v)|$, $uv\in E(F)$, are pairwise distinct. (Key special case: $F=T\sqcup K_1$, i.e. every tree with $m$ edges has an injective labelling into $\{0,\dots,m+1\}$ with distinct edge differences.)
why: Joining the c trees with c - 1 new edges makes a single tree, and a graceful labelling of that tree restricts to such a labelling of the forest. So this statement follows from the Graceful Tree Conjecture (Ringel–Kotzig–Rosa) but is weaker than it. The best unconditional results only give labels in {1,...,(1+eps)n}, or (1-eps)n distinct differences, so even one spare label for every tree would be new progress.
issues: The original hypothesis (c >= 2 and one tree with more than m/2 edges) is arbitrary. An exhaustive backtracking search over ALL forests with at most 11 vertices (475 forests at n=11) found a valid labelling for every one, with or without that hypothesis. So the hypothesis is not doing any work, and I replaced it with 'every forest'. The original version already contains the open T + K1 case (one spare label for every tree), so neither version is easy. Novelty is moderate: range-relaxed graceful labellings are studied (Van Bussel 2002; Adamaszek–Allen–Grosu–Hladký; the 2025 gracesize paper), and I did not find this exact forest formulation, but it is a natural reformulation that experts would likely regard as folklore-adjacent.

title: Sudoku transversals
W: (As posed, the claim is false when the box size n is even.) Corrected version: in every completed Sudoku with an odd box size n (for example 9x9 or 25x25), find a set of cells with exactly one in each row, each column and each symbol.
M: Original claim false for even $n$. Salvaged version: prove that every Sudoku Latin square of order $n^2$ with $n$ odd has a transversal. (This is the case of Ryser's conjecture restricted to Latin squares carrying a Sudoku (gerechte) block structure.)
why: Ryser's conjecture says every Latin square of odd order has a transversal. Montgomery proved that every large Latin square has a partial transversal of size n - 1, but full transversals in odd order remain open. Asking whether the extra Sudoku block structure forces a transversal is a natural, but much narrower, special case.
issues: FALSE as stated. Write n^2 = N and take the Cayley table of Z_N, with entry (i, j) equal to i + sigma(j) mod N, where sigma reorders the columns so that block q of columns holds q, q+n, ..., q+(n-1)n. Each n x n box then holds the sums r*n + t + q + s*n with t, s in {0..n-1}, which are all residues mod N. So every such table is a Sudoku grid, and by construction it is isotopic to the Cayley table of Z_{n^2}. For even n, Z_{n^2} has a nontrivial cyclic Sylow 2-subgroup, so its table has no transversal (Euler for the cyclic case; Hall–Paige in general), and isotopy preserves this. I verified by computer that the n=2 grid is a valid Sudoku with no transversal. For n=3 the same construction is a Sudoku and does have a transversal. With n restricted to odd values, the problem becomes a special case of the open Ryser conjecture with no clear reason why the Sudoku structure should help, so the salvaged version would be C at best.

title: Positive metric entropy for the x^4+y^4 billiard
W: The billiard table x^4 + y^4 <= 1 is smooth and convex, but its curvature vanishes at four points, so (by Mather) it has no caustics. Its phase space mixes stable islands with apparently chaotic regions. Prove that the chaos is real: on a set of positive measure, nearby trajectories separate exponentially fast.
M:
Let $\Phi$ be the billiard map of $\Omega=\{x^4+y^4\le1\}$, preserving the Liouville measure $
u=\sin	heta\,ds\,d	heta$. Prove that $h_
u(\Phi)>0$; equivalently, by Pesin's formula, that $\Phi$ has a nonzero Lyapunov exponent on a set of positive $
u$-measure.
why: Proving positive metric entropy for any smooth, area-preserving twist map with coexisting KAM islands, such as the Chirikov standard map, is a central and notoriously hard open problem. No smooth (C^2 or better) convex billiard is known to have positive metric entropy: the known examples, like stadiums and lemons, have boundary singularities. The analytic table x^4 + y^4 = 1 is the most natural concrete test case, and numerics show entropy of about 0.65 there.
issues: Not novel. Knill and coauthors studied exactly the family of billiards in l^p unit balls. They proved positive TOPOLOGICAL entropy for p not in {1, 2, infinity} and found elliptic periodic orbits, so the billiard is not ergodic. Their metric entropy estimates are numerical only, with a peak near p = 4 to 6 of about 0.65. Positive metric entropy is left open there and is a well-known open problem type. Recent progress covers topological entropy (generic analytic convex billiards, 2026; generic convex bodies, 2022) and ergodicity of asymmetric lemons (strictly convex but with corners), none of which settles this. The statement is well-posed; I made the invariant measure explicit and noted the Pesin equivalence. W's 'positive fraction is chaotic' matches 'positive Lyapunov exponent on positive measure'. One URL (Knill's html page) was blocked; the PDF was read.

title: Non-flat free-boundary minimal disks in the superball
W: In a round ball the only free-boundary minimal disks are flat slices through the centre (Nitsche). The superball x^4+y^4+z^4 <= 1 has nine flat ones, cut by its mirror planes. Is there also one that is not flat? A natural candidate has threefold symmetry about the diagonal (1,1,1).
M: For $p>2$ let $B_p=\{|x|^p+|y|^p+|z|^p\le1\}$. Decide whether $B_4$ (more generally $B_p$) contains an embedded minimal disk $\Sigma$ with $\partial\Sigma\subset\partial B_p$, meeting $\partial B_p$ orthogonally, that is not contained in a plane. Specifically, show that there is one invariant under the rotation by $2\pi/3$ about the axis $\mathbb R(1,1,1)$ and under $v\mapsto-v$.
why: Nitsche's uniqueness theorem for the round ball, together with min-max existence results for free-boundary minimal disks in convex bodies, raises the question of how many such disks a convex body has and of what kind. The superball is the simplest symmetric convex body where the answer is not forced by planes of symmetry.
issues: Web searches were unavailable for this item because the search budget was exhausted, so there is no literature check; the notes below are my own reasoning. The answer is very likely YES and probably reachable with current tools. Any disk invariant under the 3-fold rotation about (1,1,1) is automatically nonplanar, because the only invariant plane through the origin, x+y+z=0, is not a free-boundary slice: x^3+y^3+z^3 = 3xyz is not identically 0 on its boundary curve. In the round ball, the flat disk x+y+z=0 has only rotational Jacobi fields (r cos t, r sin t), and none of these is C3-invariant, so it is nondegenerate within the C3 x {±1}-equivariant class. The implicit function theorem then gives a nonplanar invariant free-boundary disk in B_p for every p close to 2. For p = 4 one would continue this branch or use equivariant min-max (Ketover-type), sweeping by the planes x+y+z=t. That makes the problem routine-to-moderate rather than deep. I sharpened M by naming the symmetric candidate and the general-p family.

title: Decidability of colouring Cayley graphs of Z^2
W: Fix a finite set D of nonzero vectors in the integer grid and join two grid points when their difference lies in D. Given D and a number of colours k, can a computer decide whether this graph can be properly coloured with k colours? On the line the answer is yes, because a colouring exists only if a periodic one does. In the plane the colourings form a tiling-type system that might have only non-periodic members.
M: For finite symmetric $D\subset\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{0\}$ let $G_D=\mathrm{Cay}(\mathbb Z^2,D)$. (a) Is the set $\{(D,k):\chi(G_D)\le k\}$ decidable? (b) Does every $k$-colourable $G_D$ admit a proper $k$-colouring that is invariant under some finite-index subgroup of $\mathbb Z^2$? A positive answer to (b) implies a positive answer to (a), since non-colourability is witnessed by a finite box (compactness) and periodic colourings can be enumerated. A negative answer to (b), i.e. a weakly aperiodic colouring system, would be of independent interest. Settle (a) or (b).
why: The k-colourings of G_D form a 2-dimensional subshift of finite type of a very special kind. General 2D SFTs can be aperiodic and have an undecidable emptiness problem (Berger), whereas 1D ones always have periodic points. So the question is whether colouring constraints coming from a group-invariant graph are rigid enough to rule out aperiodicity. This mirrors the periodic tiling conjecture, which Bhattacharya proved in Z^2 and Greenfeld–Tao disproved in high dimensions.
issues: Web searches were unavailable for this item because the search budget was exhausted, so this was not checked against the literature; it may already be posed or solved (results on periodic colourings of distance graphs and on 'domino problem' reductions to colouring are plausible prior work). Fixed a logical error: the original M called (a) and (b) 'equivalent', but (b) is only sufficient for (a). A decidable answer could coexist with aperiodic colourings. I also stated the compactness argument explicitly. The k = 2 case is trivial (bipartiteness is a parity condition, which is periodic). No counterexample attempted for k >= 3.

title: Critical NLS blow-up threshold on the cube surface
W: In the plane, the focusing cubic Schrödinger equation needs at least the ground-state mass to blow up. On the surface of a cube, each corner is a cone with total angle 3π/2, which can hold a 'three-quarter' ground state. So the blow-up threshold should drop to three quarters of the planar one, and the claim is that it does exactly that.
M: Let $S$ be the surface of the unit cube with its flat metric, and let $\Delta$ be the Friedrichs extension of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on $C_c^\infty(S\setminus\{\text{vertices}\})$. Let $Q$ be the ground state of $\Delta Q-Q+Q^3=0$ on $\mathbb R^2$, and put $m_*=\tfrac34\|Q\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}^2$. For $iu_t+\Delta u+|u|^2u=0$ on $S$, prove: (i) every $u_0\in H^1(S)$ with $\|u_0\|_2^2<m_*$ gives a global $H^1$ solution; (ii) for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $u_0\in H^1(S)$ with $m_*<\|u_0\|_2^2<m_*+\varepsilon$ whose solution blows up in finite time. (Stronger, optional: blow-up data exist for every mass $m>m_*$; also decide whether there is blow-up at mass exactly $m_*$.)
why: The sharp Gagliardo–Nirenberg constant on a cone of angle alpha <= 2*pi should be (alpha/2*pi) times the planar one, with the radial Q as extremiser. If so, conical singularities lower the mass threshold for collapse, and the cube surface turns this into a clean statement with an explicit constant. A proof would test the mass-critical blow-up theory (Weinstein, Merle–Raphaël, Burq–Gérard–Tzvetkov) on singular geometries, where existing Strichartz estimates come with loss.
issues: Web searches were unavailable for this item because the search budget was exhausted; prior work I know of (Strichartz estimates on flat cones by Ford and by Blair–Ford–Marzuola) was not re-checked. Fixes: specified the self-adjoint realisation, since on 2D cones the Laplacian on functions supported away from the vertex is not essentially self-adjoint because of the log r mode. Also replaced 'blow-up for EVERY m > 3/4||Q||^2' with 'blow-up for masses arbitrarily close above m_*'. That is the honest threshold statement, while arbitrarily large blow-up mass on a compact surface needs a separate argument, so I kept it as an optional strengthening. Part (i) looks fairly routine given a sharp GN inequality on the cone (cones with angle <= 2*pi have apex-centred disks as isoperimetric optimisers, so Polya–Szego symmetrisation should work) plus a local H^1 theory. Part (ii), building near-threshold blow-up concentrating at a vertex, is the real content.

title: Mass-critical scattering on the cube corner
W: Dodson proved that the defocusing cubic Schrödinger equation in the plane scatters for every finite-mass initial state. Show the same on the surface of an infinite cube corner, a flat cone with total angle 3π/2, where a singular point cannot be scaled away.
M: Let $\mathcal C$ be the flat cone of total angle $3\pi/2$ (isometric to the boundary of an octant), with $\Delta$ the Friedrichs extension of the Laplacian on $C_c^\infty(\mathcal C\setminus\{o\})$. Prove that for every $u_0\in L^2(\mathcal C)$ the solution of $iu_t+\Delta u=|u|^2u$ is global, has finite $L^4_{t,x}(\mathbb R\times\mathcal C)$ norm, and scatters in $L^2$ as $t\to\pm\infty$: there are $u_\pm\in L^2$ with $\|u(t)-e^{it\Delta}u_\pm\|_2\to0$.
why: Dodson's mass-critical scattering theorem relies on Euclidean translation and scaling symmetries. On a cone, scaling is still a symmetry but translation is not, and profiles concentrating at the apex rescale back to the same cone rather than to the plane. So the problem tests whether the concentration-compactness/rigidity method survives a geometry with diffraction and a fixed singular point, which is a natural step toward NLS on singular spaces.
issues: Web searches were unavailable for this item because the search budget was exhausted, so there is no literature check here. Ford's Strichartz estimates on flat cones supply the local and small-data theory, and I am not aware of a large-data mass-critical result on cones, but that is unverified. Fixes: specified the self-adjoint extension, and added the global L^4 spacetime bound, which is the standard form of the theorem. The statement is faithful to W. The difficulty is Dodson-level, so a proof would be a substantial paper. The specific angle 3*pi/2 is cosmetic: the natural statement is for all cone angles, possibly with a different mechanism for angle > 2*pi.

title: Thue–Morse Lorenz knots
W: Turn the first 2^n letters of the Thue–Morse word into a periodic orbit of the Lorenz flow, and so into a knot K_n. For n >= 4 these knots appear to be hyperbolic. Their volume grows only in proportion to n, the logarithm of the word length, not in proportion to the length itself. Prove that, and find the constant.
M: Let $K_n$ be the Lorenz knot with Lorenz word $t_0t_1\cdots t_{2^n-1}$ (the length-$2^n$ Thue–Morse prefix, $0\mapsto x$, $1\mapsto y$; this word is primitive, since Thue–Morse is overlap-free and $t_{[0,2^n)}=w\bar w$). Prove that $S^3\setminus K_n$ is hyperbolic for all $n\ge4$ and that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathrm{vol}(S^3\setminus K_n)/n$ exists and is positive. Determine the limit.
why: Lorenz knots, the periodic orbits of the Lorenz flow, are positive braids, so their volumes are tightly constrained. Asking how volume depends on the combinatorics of the generating word tests the bridge between symbolic dynamics and hyperbolic geometry. A self-similar word like Thue–Morse should yield a self-similar geometric decomposition, so the volume growth could plausibly be computed exactly.
issues: The ORIGINAL claim (vol/2^n tends to a positive limit) appears FALSE. I computed K_n as the closure of the Lorenz permutation braid of the sorted cyclic shifts and used SnapPy. n=2 gives the unknot and n=3 gives the torus knot T(3,4), with fundamental group <a,b | a^4=b^3>. For n=4..8 the knots are hyperbolic with all tetrahedra positively oriented, and the n=8 value is stable under randomisation. Volumes: 9.396, 16.184, 25.056, 32.991, 41.092. The ratios vol/2^n are 0.587, 0.506, 0.392, 0.258, 0.161, heading to 0. The increments are 6.79, 8.87, 7.93, 8.10, so roughly 8 per doubling, i.e. vol ~ 8n. That is linear in n = log2(length). This fits the picture that the hierarchical word makes large blocks of strands travel in parallel, giving about n twist regions. I rewrote W and M to the numerically supported conjecture (linear in n), set the hyperbolicity threshold to n >= 4, and added a primitivity justification. The increments may tend to about 8.12 (8 times the regular ideal tetrahedron volume), which is speculative. The family choice is arbitrary, hence grade C. Web searches were unavailable for this item because the search budget was exhausted, so there is no literature check.

title: Keller maps injective on integer points
W: Take a polynomial map of 3-space with integer coefficients whose Jacobian determinant is identically 1 (a Keller map). Show that if it never sends two different integer points to the same point, then it is a polynomial automorphism.
M: Let $F\in\mathbb{Z}[x,y,z]^3$ with $\det JF\equiv 1$. Prove that if $F|_{\mathbb{Z}^3}$ is injective, then $F$ has a polynomial inverse (equivalently, by Bia{\l}ynicki-Birula--Rosenlicht, $F$ is injective on $\mathbb{C}^3$).
why: This is a weak form of the Jacobian conjecture in dimension 3, and the conjecture itself would make it vacuous. Its interest is the arithmetic angle: Siegel's theorem on integral points has already produced invertibility criteria for Keller maps over Z, and those criteria are phrased in terms of integral points on fibres.
issues: This is strictly implied by JC(3), which is open, so it is open too, but I found no technique that uses injectivity on Z^3 at all. Reduction mod p and Ax-Grothendieck need injectivity over finite fields or algebraically closed fields, not over Z. Choosing n=3 is arbitrary, since n=2 is open as well. I found no literature that states this exact hypothesis. The nearest work gives JC criteria from integral points on fibres (Siegel's theorem). It feels like a hybrid of JC with an unmotivated extra hypothesis, with no visible route that avoids JC itself. The W wording was clarified.

title: Fibonacci-modulated growing Jacobi matrix
W: Take a Jacobi matrix with zero diagonal and off-diagonal weights sqrt(n). Double the weight at every position where the Fibonacci word has a 1. Periodic modulations of power-growing weights are known to produce spectral phase transitions. Determine the spectral type for this aperiodic modulation.
M: Let $f=f_1f_2f_3\cdots=0100101001001\cdots\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ be the Fibonacci word, the fixed point of $0\mapsto01,\ 1\mapsto0$. Let $J$ be the Jacobi operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ with $(Ju)_n=a_{n-1}u_{n-1}+a_nu_{n+1}$, where $a_n=\sqrt n\,(1+f_n)$ and $a_0u_0:=0$. Since $\sum 1/a_n=\infty$, $J$ is self-adjoint (Carleman). Determine the spectral type of $J$. In particular: is $\sigma_{ac}(J)\neq\emptyset$? Is $\sigma_{ac}(J)=\mathbb R$? Is the spectrum on some interval pure point or singular continuous?
why: Janas, Naboko, Swiderski and others classified unbounded Jacobi matrices with periodically modulated power-growing weights. Whether the spectrum is absolutely continuous, a gap, or point spectrum is decided by the trace of a single period's transfer matrix. A Fibonacci modulation joins this theory to the trace-map dynamics of quasicrystal Schrodinger operators. In that setting the period matrix is replaced by a hierarchy of block products.
issues: I found no literature on aperiodic or Sturmian modulations of unbounded weights, only periodic ones (Janas-Naboko, Swiderski, Naboko-Simonov). Heuristic: with b=0 and lambda/a_n -> 0, two-step transfer matrices are close to diag(-a_{n-1}/a_n, -a_{n-2}/a_{n-1}). Their products are governed by D_N=sum_{k<=N}(f_{2k-1}-f_{2k}). Numerically |D_N| grows like log N (records +-10 by N=10^6, about one unit per factor phi^3), so 2^{D_N} is roughly N^{0.47}. That is close to the l^2 borderline, and it competes with the O(sqrt N) phase rotation from lambda/a_n. So the answer is not obvious. I fixed the indexing and the convention for the Fibonacci word, and added the self-adjointness remark. The choices of exponent 1/2 and factor 2 are somewhat arbitrary.

title: Smallest force for blow-up
W: How weak can a force be and still make an initially resting viscous fluid blow up?
M: (Ill-posed as stated.) A meaningful repair must fix the domain (say $\mathbb T^3$ with period $1$), the force class (say $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb T^3\times[0,\infty))$), and a scale-invariant measure of force size. Even then the infimum is over a set not known to be nonempty in the periodic setting.
why: Not recommended.
issues: 1) On R^3 the scaling u_l(x,t)=l u(lx,l^2 t), f_l=l^3 f(lx,l^2 t) keeps nu fixed and sends ||f||_inf to 0. So if any blow-up with a bounded force exists, the infimum is 0 for every nu and no exponent a is defined. 2) The scaling u -> nu u, f -> nu^2 f relates different viscosities exactly, so on a domain with a fixed length scale the answer is a=2 by dimensional analysis, provided the infimum is positive and finite. That is either trivial or reduces to an unknown constant. 3) Domain, force class (time-dependent? smooth? compact support?) and the meaning of 'blows up' are all unspecified. 4) Recent constructions of forced blow-up (Q. S. Zhang, critical-order forces; Lei-Ren expositions of smooth-force constructions on R^3) settle existence on R^3, and with scaling that makes the R^3 infimum 0.

title: Hadwiger's true constant
W: Among graphs whose chromatic number is at least t, what is the largest complete-graph minor they are all guaranteed to contain, as a fraction of t, when t is large? Hadwiger's conjecture says the fraction is 1. It is not even known to be bounded away from 0.
M: Let $h(G)$ be the Hadwiger number (largest $s$ with $K_s\preceq G$). Determine $c^*=\liminf_{t\to\infty}\ \inf\{h(G)/t:\ \chi(G)\ge t\}$. Trivially $c^*\le 1$, and Hadwiger's conjecture gives $c^*=1$. The known bound $\chi=O(t\log\log\log t)$ on $K_t$-minor-free graphs still only gives $c^*\ge 0$. In particular, is $c^*>0$?
why: This is the linear (asymptotic) form of Hadwiger's conjecture, one of the central problems in graph theory. The question c*>0 is the well-known Linear Hadwiger Conjecture.
issues: NOT NOVEL. This is a restatement of a famous open problem. 'Is c*>0' is exactly the linear Hadwiger conjecture, and 'c*=1' is the asymptotic Hadwiger conjecture. The original W presupposed that Hadwiger is false, so I rewrote it. 'min' should be 'inf'. Current record: chi(G)=O(t log log log t) for K_t-minor-free graphs (Liu-Luo 2026), improving Delcourt-Postle O(t log log t). Include only if the list allows classic problems. Otherwise drop.

title: 3-SAT at density 4
W: Give a polynomial-time algorithm that, with probability tending to 1, finds a satisfying assignment of a uniformly random 3-SAT formula with n variables and 4n clauses.
M: Let $\Phi$ be a uniformly random 3-CNF formula with $n$ variables and $m=\lfloor 4n\rfloor$ clauses (independent uniform clauses on 3 distinct variables). Give a (possibly randomized) polynomial-time algorithm that outputs a satisfying assignment of $\Phi$ with probability $1-o(1)$. Note that this would in particular prove $r_3\ge 4$ for the satisfiability threshold, whereas the best rigorous lower bound is $r_3\ge 3.52$.
why: Random 3-SAT shows a large gap between where efficient algorithms provably succeed (about 3.52) and the conjectured threshold (about 4.267). Survey propagation appears to work up to about 4.2 in experiments, but nothing has been proved. Closing even part of this gap for k=3 would be a major advance on the 'statistical vs computational gap' programme.
issues: Not novel: the algorithmic gap for random 3-SAT is a well-known open problem, and 4.0 is an arbitrary point inside it. Note the hidden strength. Satisfiability at density 4 is not even proven (best rigorous lower bound 3.52, Kaporis-Kirousis-Lalas and Hajiaghayi-Sorkin; upper bound about 4.49), so a solution would also improve the threshold lower bound. I made the model explicit. A more natural version asks for the largest density reachable by some provable polynomial-time algorithm, or for a proof that survey-propagation-guided decimation works at a given density.

title: Ergodicity of the regular tetrahedron billiard
W: A billiard ball bounces inside a regular tetrahedron. The tetrahedron does not tile space, and its dihedral angle arccos(1/3) is an irrational multiple of pi. So the billiard cannot be unfolded into a straight-line flow on a torus or a translation structure. Is the motion ergodic, so that almost every trajectory equidistributes in position and direction?
M: Let $\Delta\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a regular tetrahedron and $\phi_t$ the billiard flow on the unit tangent bundle $T^1\Delta$, with specular reflection at faces and orbits hitting edges or vertices discarded (a null set). Prove or disprove that $\phi_t$ is ergodic with respect to Liouville measure.
why: Ergodicity of billiards in irrational polygons is open even in the plane. No explicit irrational triangle is known to be ergodic, although Kerckhoff-Masur-Smillie and Vorobets show that generic polygons are. The regular tetrahedron is the most symmetric and canonical non-rational polyhedron, so it is the natural first test case for polyhedral billiards. In that setting the group generated by reflection linear parts is infinite, which rules out the translation-surface methods.
issues: Open as far as I can tell. The literature on tetrahedral billiards covers periodic orbits (Fagnano-type orbits, Bedaride and others) and 'uniformity' results for special polyhedra built from 2D (Beck et al.). I found nothing on ergodicity of the regular tetrahedron. The statement is clean. I added the treatment of singular orbits. Caveat: this is probably far beyond current techniques, since even a single explicit ergodic irrational triangle is unknown. A related, perhaps more tractable variant: is the flow topologically transitive, or are there only countably many periodic directions?

title: Geodesic squares on convex surfaces
W: On a smooth convex surface, measure distance by the length of the shortest path on the surface. Every smooth simple closed curve on the surface should contain four points that form a 'square' in this sense: four equal sides and two equal diagonals.
M: Let $S=\partial K$ for a convex body $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ with smooth boundary and positive Gaussian curvature, and let $d$ be the intrinsic distance on $S$. Prove that every smooth simple closed curve $\gamma\subset S$ contains four distinct points $p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4$, in this cyclic order along $\gamma$, with $d(p_1,p_2)=d(p_2,p_3)=d(p_3,p_4)=d(p_4,p_1)>0$ and $d(p_1,p_3)=d(p_2,p_4)$.
why: This is the Toeplitz square peg problem moved from the plane to intrinsic geometry. In the plane the smooth case is classical (Schnirelmann), and there are strong recent results (Greene-Lobb rectangles). Recent work extends inscription theorems to constant-curvature surfaces: the hyperbolic plane, and spheres for curves disjoint from their antipodal image. A general convex surface tests whether the topological parity argument survives variable curvature and a non-smooth distance function (cut loci).
issues: Original M said 'geodesic quadrilateral' without defining it, and it did not exclude degenerate squares or fix the cyclic order. I fixed all three. I found no paper treating general convex surfaces. Naseri Sadr 2025 covers the constant-curvature cases (could not open the page to check details). For curves inside a strongly convex geodesic ball the standard Schnirelmann parity argument probably adapts. The real difficulty is long curves whose would-be diagonals cross the cut locus, where d is not smooth. Likely true. Moderate interest.

title: Deciding limit cycles
W: Given a polynomial vector field in the plane with rational coefficients, is there an algorithm that decides whether it has a limit cycle, that is, an isolated closed orbit? Hilbert's 16th problem asks how many limit cycles there can be. This asks only whether their existence is algorithmically decidable. The same question can be asked for closed orbits of any kind, including those in period annuli around centres.
M: Let $\mathcal L=\{(P,Q)\in\mathbb Q[x,y]^2:\ \dot x=P,\ \dot y=Q$ has a limit cycle in $\mathbb R^2\}$ and $\mathcal P=\{(P,Q)\in\mathbb Q[x,y]^2:$ the system has a non-constant periodic orbit in $\mathbb R^2\}$, with polynomials encoded by their lists of rational coefficients. (a) Is $\mathcal L$ decidable? (b) Is $\mathcal P$ decidable? (c) Are $\mathcal L$, $\mathcal P$ or their complements at least recursively enumerable?
why: Poincare-Bendixson confines planar dynamics so strongly that undecidability constructions which work in dimension 3 and higher (polynomial ODEs simulating Turing machines) do not apply. Known noncomputability results for counting periodic orbits (Graca-Zhong) use real computable coefficients and discontinuity, not exact rational input. So decidability of existence is a sharp test of whether planar polynomial dynamics is 'algorithmically tame'. Part (b) is tied to the center-focus problem, which Il'yashenko showed is not algebraically solvable.
issues: Literature: Graca-Zhong (Computing the exact number of periodic orbits for planar flows) show that the map from a polynomial field to its number of periodic orbits is noncomputable. But their families have computable real, not rational, coefficients, and the result concerns counting, not existence. Earlier Graca-Buescu-Campagnolo give semi-decidability of hyperbolic periodic orbits for structurally stable systems and leave decidability open. I found no paper settling (a) or (b) for rational input. Not tied to a specific degree, so (a) and (b) are uniform questions. Note that for each fixed degree, center conditions are given by a finitely generated Bautin ideal, so non-uniform questions can become trivially 'decidable'. Hence the uniform encoding matters. I added (c) as a natural weaker form. Hyperbolic limit cycles can be certified by interval methods, so 'has a hyperbolic limit cycle' is r.e. The hard cases are non-hyperbolic cycles and proving non-existence.

why: Advection and vortex stretching are the same size under scaling, and their competition decides regularity in 1D Euler models. In the De Gregorio, Cordoba-Cordoba-Fontelos and Okamoto-Sakajo-Wunsch models, the sign and relative weight of stretching flip the answer between blow-up and regularity (Elgindi-Jeong). title: Shifted Fujita equation
W: In the plane, every positive solution of u_t = Delta u + u^2 blows up (u^2 is exactly Fujita-critical in dimension 2). Does this survive when u^2 is replaced by the product of the values of u one unit to the left and one unit to the right?
M: Let $e=(1,0)$. Prove or disprove: for every $0\le u_0\in C_c(\mathbb R^2)$ with $u_0\not\equiv0$, the solution of $u_t=\Delta u+u(x-e,t)\,u(x+e,t)$ on $\mathbb R^2$ blows up in finite time.
why: This tests how robust the Fujita phenomenon is at the critical exponent p=1+2/n when the nonlinearity is non-local in space. It is a small model of delayed or shifted interactions.
issues: Likely true with a routine proof. The nonlinearity is monotone in u, so comparison and Duhamel lower bounds hold. For Gaussian lower bounds u(s) >= a(s) g_s, the shift costs only the constant factor e^{-|e|^2/(2s)} >= e^{-1/2} for s >= 1, because g_s(x-e) g_s(x+e) = g_s(x)^2 e^{-1/(2s)}. The standard critical-case iteration (Weissler, Kobayashi-Sirao-Tanaka) is insensitive to constant factors in front of u^2. So the classical proof should go through with minor changes (restrict to the parabolic region |x|^2 <= t). No specific literature found, but the problem looks like an exercise.

title: Keller monodromy is everything
W: Since 2026 there are polynomial maps of 3-space with constant nonzero Jacobian that are not invertible (counterexamples to the Jacobian conjecture), and every number n >= 3 of points in a generic fibre occurs. Show that for every n the fibre points can be permuted in every possible way by going around loops, i.e. the monodromy group can be the full symmetric group S_n.
M: Prove that for every $n\ge3$ there is a polynomial map $F:\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^3$ with $\det JF\in\mathbb C^{\times}$, of geometric degree $[\mathbb C(x):\mathbb C(F)]=n$, whose geometric monodromy group (the Galois group of the Galois closure of $\mathbb C(x_1,x_2,x_3)/\mathbb C(F_1,F_2,F_3)$, acting on the $n$ generic fibre points) is $S_n$.
why: After Alpöge's 2026 counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture in dimension 3, the natural invariants of a non-invertible Keller map are its geometric degree and the monodromy of its generic fibre; realising the full symmetric group in every degree would show these maps are as 'generic' as branched covers can be. It is a clean test of how flexible the new constructions are.
issues: Original M omitted the precise meaning of 'monodromy group' (now defined as the geometric Galois group). Literature (2026 preprints) already covers much of it: S_3 for Alpöge's map (arXiv 2607.20210, Thm 4.4); graded families with monodromy S_N for N=kd, k odd>=3, d>=3, and S_{2r-1} for r even (N = 3 mod 4), A_N in other cases, and S_12 for a quartic-seed member (arXiv 2608.02863); Gallagher's family realises every degree n>=3 but its monodromy is not computed; 'ordinary weighted lifts' have S_N monodromy by a Morse-degeneration argument (arXiv 2609.33491, Prop 7.1). Remaining cases (e.g. n=4,5,6,8,10) look routine: one transposition plus primitivity via a Morse degeneration of the fibre polynomial. Not elite; probably closes quickly.

title: Formal verification depth of RH
W: Is the Riemann hypothesis provable in very weak systems of arithmetic, such as elementary function arithmetic?
M: Decide whether the $\Pi^0_1$ form of RH (e.g. Lagarias' inequality $\sigma(n)\le H_n+e^{H_n}\log H_n$ for all $n$) is provable in $\mathrm{I}\Sigma_1$, or in $\mathrm{EFA}=\mathrm{I}\Delta_0+\exp$.
why: Friedman's 'grand conjecture' predicts that essentially all of ordinary number theory, RH included if true, is provable in EFA; RH is a concrete Pi^0_1 test case. But as a problem it is at least as hard as RH itself.
issues: Premise in W is false: RH has no Lean proof (2026 Lean work concerns zeta formalisation and a better critical-line proportion / 'quasi-RH', not RH). Fatal flaw: a false Pi^0_1 sentence is refutable already in Robinson's Q, so ANY resolution (provable, or unprovable i.e. consistent) implies RH is true. Hence the question strictly contains RH and, if RH is proved by ordinary means, the 'provable in EFA' direction is the expected routine bookkeeping covered by Friedman's grand conjecture. Not a reasonable list item.

title: Monochromatic square-sum triangles, many colours
W: Colour the positive integers with finitely many colours. Show there are always three different numbers of the same colour whose three pairwise sums are all perfect squares.
M: Prove that for every $r\ge1$ and every colouring $\chi:\mathbb N\to\{1,\dots,r\}$ there exist distinct $a,b,c\in\mathbb N$ with $\chi(a)=\chi(b)=\chi(c)$ and $a+b,\ a+c,\ b+c$ all perfect squares.
