(Equivalently: the triangle hypergraph of the graph on $\mathbb N$ with $a\sim b\iff a+b=\square$ has infinite chromatic number.)
why: Khalfalah and Szemeredi proved that every finite colouring has a monochromatic pair x != y with x+y a square; this asks for the next configuration, a monochromatic triangle in the 'square-sum graph'. Density arguments fail (residue classes such as n = 1 mod 3 contain no such triangle), so a proof must be genuinely Ramsey-theoretic, in the same family as the open Pythagorean-triple and {x,y,x+y,xy} problems.
issues: Statement clean; colouring renamed to chi to avoid a clash with the element c. Not found posed in the literature (checked Khalfalah-Szemeredi line, Pach's x+y=z^2 work, Di Nasso-Luperi Baglini style surveys). Local (p-adic) obstructions do not kill it: for each prime one residue/valuation class survives. Quick SAT check (CaDiCaL): a 2-colouring of {1..8000} avoiding such triangles exists, but none exists for {1..10000}, so the r=2 case holds with threshold in (8000,10000]; r>=3 is open computationally. Natural but somewhat specialised; B.

title: Computable connective constants
W: Count the self-avoiding walks of length n on the Cayley graph of a finitely generated group. Their n-th roots decrease to the connective constant, so it can always be approximated from above. For groups with a solvable word problem, can it always be computed to any precision, i.e. also approximated from below?
M: Let $G$ be a finitely generated group with solvable word problem, $S=S^{-1}$ a finite generating set, $c_n$ the number of $n$-step self-avoiding walks from $e$ in $\mathrm{Cay}(G,S)$, and $\mu(G,S)=\lim_n c_n^{1/n}=\inf_n c_n^{1/n}$ (a right-computable real). Is $\mu(G,S)$ always a computable real? If not, construct $(G,S)$ with solvable word problem and $\mu(G,S)$ non-computable. If so, is the map (word-problem algorithm, $S$) $\mapsto\mu(G,S)$ uniformly computable?
why: The connective constant is the basic growth rate of self-avoiding walks; for graphs with a (unimodular) graph height function, bridge counts are supermultiplicative and give matching lower bounds, so mu is computable for e.g. solvable groups with solvable word problem. Whether this can fail when no height function exists (Higman-type groups, torsion groups such as Grigorchuk's) ties the probabilistic theory of SAWs on groups to computability and symbolic dynamics, where entropies of effective subshifts are exactly the right-computable reals.
issues: Statement precise; inf=lim holds by submultiplicativity on transitive graphs. Known: mu is right computable for recursively presented groups (Aubrun-Bitar 2023, cited as Lemma 4.11 in arXiv 2402.13944); log mu is the entropy of the SAW 'skeleton' subshift; computable (Perron-number powers) for plain groups; lower bounds via bridges for Cayley graphs with graph height functions (Grimmett-Li), covering all f.g. solvable groups. The general question (left-computability without height functions) does not appear posed. A negative answer would need a group with solvable word problem whose SAW growth encodes a non-computable left limit, plausible via Dehn-monster or torsion constructions; neither direction looks easy. Specialised audience; B.

title: Three identical vortices on a square torus are chaotic
W: On a flat torus, three point vortices with total circulation zero form an integrable system (Stremler-Aref), but for vortices of equal strength even three are believed chaotic, from numerics only. Prove that three identical point vortices on the square torus are not integrable; the same question is open for four.
M: Let $G$ be the Green function of $\mathbb T=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z)$ ($\Delta G=\delta_0-1$) and $H=-\sum_{i<j}G(z_i-z_j)$ on $\{(z_1,\dots,z_N)\in\mathbb T^N: z_i\ne z_j\}$ with symplectic form $\sum_i dx_i\wedge dy_i$. The centre $Z=\sum_i z_i\in\mathbb T$ is conserved; the reduced space $M_N=\{Z=Z_0\}/(\tfrac1N\mathbb Z[i]/\mathbb Z[i])$ is symplectic of dimension $2N-2$. Prove that for $N=3$ the reduced flow on $M_3$ has no real-analytic first integral functionally independent of $H$ (and likewise for $N=4$ on $M_4$).
why: Point-vortex systems are the standard finite-dimensional models of 2D Euler; integrability is classified on the plane, sphere and for zero total circulation on the torus, but for nonzero circulation on the torus the translation momenta do not commute and only N=2 is integrable. Proving non-integrability for N=3 identical vortices would be the first rigorous chaos result for vortex lattices, where only numerics (Borisov-Mamaev-Kilin) exist.
issues: W's premise was false for identical vortices: Stremler-Aref integrability of three vortices in a periodic parallelogram requires zero total circulation; with nonzero total circulation only N=2 is integrable (survey arXiv 2003.00716, Thm 7) and N=3 is numerically nonintegrable (Borisov-Mamaev-Kilin, RCD 2019). Hence the original 'four identical' version skipped the first open case; restated with N=3 as main case. Clarified the reduction: Z in T is a genuine conserved quantity, translation by 1/N-lattice points acts on its level set, reduced dimension 2N-2 (P_x,P_y do not Poisson-commute, so translations remove only one degree of freedom). Also fixed Green-function normalisation (uniform background). Likely approach: Ziglin/Morales-Ramis along a collinear or symmetric invariant family, or Melnikov splitting; technical but feasible.

title: Translative Lebesgue covering
W: Find the convex shape of least area that contains a translated copy of every planar set of diameter 1, when only translations (no rotations or reflections) are allowed. Is the Jung disc of radius 1/sqrt(3), which is optimal for perimeter, also optimal for area?
M: Let $\mathcal D$ be the family of planar sets of diameter at most $1$. Determine $\alpha=\min\{\mathrm{area}(K): K\subset\mathbb R^2 \text{ convex},\ \forall X\in\mathcal D\ \exists t\in\mathbb R^2: X+t\subseteq K\}$ and all minimisers up to translation. In particular decide whether $\alpha<\pi/3$ (the area of the disc of radius $1/\sqrt3$).
why: Lebesgue's universal-cover problem (rigid motions allowed) is a century old and still unsolved; the translation-only version is the natural rigid analogue of Pal's solution of the convex Kakeya problem (equilateral triangle of height 1) and of Bezdek-Connelly's theorem that the disc of radius 1/sqrt3 is the unique minimum-perimeter translation cover of diameter-1 sets. Its answer measures how much rotation actually helps in Lebesgue's problem.
issues: Original title 'Hexagonal' was unjustified: a fixed regular hexagon of width 1 does not contain translates of all rotated Reuleaux triangles (Pal's hexagon argument uses rotation). Uniqueness claim replaced by 'determine all minimisers up to translation' (uniqueness unproven and unmotivated). Existence of a minimiser follows from Blaschke selection. Literature: perimeter version solved (Bezdek-Connelly; cited in arXiv 1209.2171); area version for diameter-1 sets not found solved; related translation/discrete-rotation covers for curves and segments in Jung-Yoon-Ahn-Tokuyama (Adv. Geom. 2023). Bounds: alpha >= area of min translation cover of unit segments and unit disc together; alpha <= pi/3. Quick numerics: translating 6 rotated copies of the width-1 Reuleaux triangle by optimized offsets gives hull area ~0.978 < centred 1.026, so the centred disc is likely not area-optimal, i.e. the answer is probably a non-trivial shape.

title: Firebreak with wind
W: A fire starts at a point and spreads faster downwind: its front moves at speed a + b cos(theta) in direction theta (0 <= b < a). Firefighters can build a barrier at total rate sigma (length per unit time), anywhere, and the fire cannot cross it. For which sigma can the fire be confined to a bounded region?
M: Let the reachable set of the free fire from $R_0=\{0\}$ be $tF$, where $F=\{r(\cos\theta,\sin\theta): 0\le r\le a+b\cos\theta\}$ (convexified if necessary), $0\le b<a$. A barrier is a rectifiable set $\Gamma=\bigcup_t\gamma(t)$ with $\mathcal H^1(\gamma(t)\cap\overline{R(t)})\le\sigma t$ (Bressan's admissibility), where $R(t)$ is the set reachable from $R_0$ by paths with velocity in $F$ avoiding $\Gamma$. Determine $\sigma^*(a,b)=\inf\{\sigma: \exists$ admissible $\Gamma$ with $\bigcup_t R(t)$ bounded$\}$, or at least its asymptotics as $b/a\to1$.
why: This is the anisotropic (wind-driven) version of Bressan's fire-confinement problem, whose isotropic threshold is still open (conjectured sigma* = 2, known only 1.626 <= sigma* <= 2). Wind is the realistic case for wildfires and makes the geometry of optimal barriers genuinely asymmetric.
issues: Original M was ill-posed: fire origin, wind direction relative to the town, where/when the barrier may be built, and what 'protects' means were unspecified. In its natural reading it is near-trivial: since an unconfined fire eventually covers the plane, the cheapest protection is a closed curve around the convex town, so the minimal length is essentially its perimeter whenever the time budget allows, and otherwise infeasible. Replaced by the anisotropic blocking-threshold question. That version is meaningful but derivative: it contains the open isotropic case (b=0) and anisotropic convex speed profiles are already in Bressan's framework (differential inclusions with convex velocity sets), so it is unlikely to be novel or elite.

title: Spikes at the primes
W: Put a bump of fixed height at every prime on the half-line lattice and study the electron (discrete Schrodinger operator). What kind of spectrum does it have inside the free band (-2,2)? If the primes behaved like a random sparse set (Cramer model), the states would be localized (pure point spectrum); is that true for the actual primes?
M: Let $(Hu)(n)=u(n+1)+u(n-1)+\lambda\mathbf 1_{\mathbb P}(n)u(n)$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ with Dirichlet condition $u(0)=0$, $\lambda\ne0$. Determine the spectral type of $H$ on $(-2,2)$. In particular: is the spectral measure restricted to $(-2,2)$ pure point (with exponentially or sub-exponentially decaying eigenfunctions), or does it have a singular continuous part, e.g. near $E=0$?
why: It is the cleanest deterministic test of whether the primes are 'pseudo-random' for spectral theory: the random sparse model with site density 1/log n localizes, while deterministic sparse potentials typically produce singular continuous spectrum. The answer must use arithmetic input (distribution of primes in residue classes and gaps), linking Schrodinger operators to analytic number theory.
issues: No absolutely continuous spectrum is automatic: 1_P takes finitely many values and is not eventually periodic, so Remling's theorem (Annals 2011) gives Sigma_ac = empty; hence the content is pure point vs singular continuous. The conjectured pure-point answer is doubtful: numerics in the 2001 study 'De(Localization) in the Prime Schrodinger Operator' (cond-mat/0103313) report a persistent delocalized band near E=0 of width ~1/lambda. Simple check: at E=0 the recursion decouples by parity and, since all primes but 2 are odd, solutions grow only like partial sums of chi_4(p) (polynomially), not like the random model; analogous arithmetic resonances occur at E=2cos(pi a/q). So 'prove pure point' was replaced by 'determine the spectral type'. The question is posed (numerically) in the literature, so novelty is low; difficulty likely very high. Literature search for rigorous results was cut short by the search budget.

title: Heat with a cosine reaction
W: In u_t = u_xx + cos(x) u^2 the reaction term averages to zero over a period, but a second-order (homogenization) effect produces an effective +u^3 term, which in one dimension is exactly Fujita's borderline exponent where every positive solution of u_t = u_xx + u^3 blows up. Does every positive solution of the cosine equation blow up in finite time?
M: Prove or disprove: for every $u_0\in C_c(\mathbb R)$ with $u_0\ge0$, $u_0\not\equiv0$, the classical solution of $u_t=u_{xx}+\cos(x)\,u^2$, $u(\cdot,0)=u_0$, blows up in finite time. (More generally, for $a\in C^\infty(\mathbb T^d)$ with $\int a=0$, $a\not\equiv0$, show the Fujita exponent of $u_t=\Delta u+a(x)u^p$ is $p^*=1+1/d$: all positive solutions blow up for $1<p\le p^*$, small ones are global for $p>p^*$.)
why: Fujita's theorem is the prototype of 'all solutions blow up vs. small data global' thresholds; with a sign-changing, mean-zero weight the first-order effect cancels and the threshold is set by a homogenized second-order term $c\,v^{2p-1}$ with $c=\langle a,(-\Delta)^{-1}a\rangle>0$, predicting $p^*=1+1/d$. The posed equation is exactly the critical case $d=1,p=2$, where standard test-function/Kaplan arguments fail because the weight changes sign.
issues: Well-posed: positivity is preserved (linear comparison with coefficient cos(x)u), and large data blow up by comparison with the Dirichlet problem on (-pi/3,pi/3) where cos >= 1/2, so only small/spread data matter. Checked the homogenization: u ~ v + cos(x)v^2 gives effective v_t = v_xx + v^3 (coefficient 2<cos^2>=1), first-order oscillatory corrections average out, and next-order terms are integrable in time against the t^{-1} log-divergence of the critical case, so the conjectured answer is 'yes, all blow up'. Added the general-d, general-p formulation. Known results I recall (Pinsky 1997 for a(x) ~ |x|^m >= 0; Meier on bounded domains) do not cover periodic mean-zero weights; literature check was limited because the search budget ran out, so novelty is moderately uncertain.

title: Strauss exponent for an oscillating source
W: The 3D wave equation with source |u|^p has small-data global solutions exactly when p exceeds the Strauss exponent 1+sqrt2. If the source is multiplied by cos t, the usual blow-up proofs (which need a positive source) break, and time-oscillation may cancel the source. What is the new threshold?
M: For $u_{tt}-\Delta u=\cos(t)\,|u|^p$ on $\mathbb R^{1+3}$, $p>1$, with data $(u,u_t)(0)=\varepsilon(f,g)$, $f,g\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, let $p_c=\inf\{p>1:$ for all $f,g$ the solution is global for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0\}$. Determine $p_c$, and show that for $1<p<p_c$ there are $f,g$ for which global existence fails for all small $\varepsilon$ (or the lifespan is finite). Is $p_c=2$ (parametric-resonance prediction) rather than $1+\sqrt2$?
why: Strauss' conjecture (now a theorem) is a central small-data threshold for nonlinear waves; all blow-up proofs use positivity of the source, so a sign-changing time-periodic factor tests which mechanism really sets the threshold. Heuristics suggest a different answer from Strauss, governed by resonance between the forcing frequency and the waves rather than by the size of the source.
issues: Original M presupposed a sharp dichotomy exponent (existence of p_c with blow-up below and global above), which need not hold; redefined p_c as an infimum and framed the blow-up side as failure of small-data global existence (growth could be infinite-time). Heuristics: near the light cone u ~ F(r-t)/r; integrating cos t |F|^p r^{1-p} along outgoing characteristics gives oscillatory cancellation, and the second-order averaged term (cos t * sin t) also averages to 0, so the Strauss/John iteration mechanism is suppressed. But |u|^{p-1} acts as a time-periodic potential cos(t) V with V ~ r^{1-p} on the shell, producing Mathieu-type resonance at frequency 1/2 with amplification exp(c int r^{1-p} dt), divergent iff p <= 2; this suggests p_c = 2, not 1+sqrt2. Not found in literature, but the search budget ran out before a dedicated search for time-dependent oscillating coefficients (literature on g(t)|u|^p usually takes g >= 0 or of power type), so novelty is uncertain.

title: Minimal degree of a Jacobian counterexample
W: The 2026 counterexamples to the Jacobian conjecture in three variables have degree 7 at best (Alpöge's map has component degrees 7,6,4). Wang's theorem says degree 2 is impossible. Find the smallest degree a three-variable counterexample can have: some number from 3 to 7.
M: Call $F=(F_1,F_2,F_3)\in\mathbb C[x,y,z]^3$ a Keller map if $\det JF\in\mathbb C^{\times}$, and set $\deg F=\max_i\deg F_i$. Determine $d_3=\min\{\deg F: F \text{ a Keller map that is not injective on }\mathbb C^3\}$. Known: $3\le d_3\le 7$ (Wang: degree $\le2$ Keller maps are invertible in every dimension; Alpöge, van den Essen: explicit degree-7 examples). In particular, is every cubic Keller map $\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^3$ invertible?
why: Now that the Jacobian conjecture is known to fail in dimension 3, the obvious next question is how small a failure can be. The minimal degree marks the line between low-degree regimes where invertibility can still be proved (Wang's degree-2 theorem, cubic-homogeneous results in small dimension) and the region where counterexamples exist. Because the Bass–Connell–Wright reduction raises the dimension, the cubic case in dimension 3 is a genuinely separate question.
issues: The original said 'the 2026 counterexamples have degree 7'. That is accurate for Alpöge's F (7,6,4) and van den Essen's (7,5,4), but Gallagher-type examples have higher degree, so I reworded it to 'degree 7 at best'. I defined 'Keller map' and 'degree' (max component degree, as opposed to geometric degree) and stated the known bounds 3<=d_3<=7. I found no paper that determines d_3 or settles the general cubic case in C^3, but the question is probably being actively studied. It is also a finite-dimensional algebraic problem for each degree, so computer searches may settle it soon, which lowers its long-term novelty.

title: Fluid in a box blows up
W: Show that a viscous fluid in a closed box with sticky walls can blow up in finite time under a smooth push.
M: Construct $u_0\in C_c^\infty((0,1)^3)$, divergence-free, and $f\in C^\infty([0,1]^3\times[0,T))$ such that the 3D Navier–Stokes solution in the unit cube with no-slip boundary condition becomes singular as $t\uparrow T$.
why: This would be the bounded-domain, no-slip version of the 2026 forced blow-up of Navier–Stokes. Since that blow-up can be localised, the bounded-domain version is a corollary, not a new problem.
issues: This is already known, and it is close to trivial. OpenAI's 2026 construction gives blow-up from zero data with a force in C_c^infty(R^3 x (0,inf)). Cao–Chi–Nie (arXiv 2609.10262, Cor. 3.14 and Prop. 3.16) glue such a blow-up into an interior ball of a bounded box or smooth domain with no-slip boundary, and Prop. 3.16 starts from zero initial velocity. More simply, cut off the stream function of the R^3 blow-up solution near the singular point. This gives a compactly supported, divergence-free velocity that blows up, and its Navier–Stokes residual is a force that is smooth on [0,T) and vanishes near the walls. As stated, the problem has no content beyond these results.

title: Unforced blow-up near the forced one
W: The 2026 forced Navier–Stokes blow-up uses a force that is smooth through the blow-up time. Can the force be made to vanish identically at the blow-up instant while staying smooth up to and including that instant?
M: Do there exist $T>0$ and $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times(0,\infty))$ with $f(\cdot,T)\equiv0$ such that the 3D Navier–Stokes solution on $\mathbb R^3$ with $u_0=0$ and force $f$ satisfies $\limsup_{t\uparrow T}\|u(t)\|_{L^\infty}=\infty$? (Requiring $f\equiv0$ on $[T-\delta,T]$ for some $\delta>0$ instead would be equivalent to unforced blow-up from smooth data, which is the Millennium problem.)
why: Requiring the force to vanish at the blow-up time is a small step from forced blow-up toward unforced blow-up. It tests whether the OpenAI construction really needs active forcing at the singular moment. The construction's force is already flat at the singular point, so this refinement asks whether the rest of the forcing can be switched off in time as well.
issues: As originally stated (f smooth only on [0,T), with ||f(t)||_{L^2}->0), the problem is close to routine. The OpenAI force is C_c^infty in space-time and vanishes to infinite order at the singular point. Set v=u+phi(t)h with h=-P f(.,T) and phi(T)=0, phi'(T)=1. The residual of v is then a force that is smooth on [0,T), and its L^2 norm tends to 0 if tau*||grad u(t)||_2 -> 0, which the self-similar scaling should give. So I tightened M to require f smooth through T with f(.,T)=0. Even that version is a technical variant of a known construction, and it does not approach the unforced problem.

title: Spikes at the squares
W: On the half-line lattice, add a fixed spike of height λ at every perfect square. The free band (-2,2) then has no absolutely continuous spectrum, by Remling's theorem. Decide whether the spectrum inside the band is pure point (localized states) or singular continuous. A heuristic in the physics literature predicts singular continuous.
M: Let $(Hu)(n)=u(n+1)+u(n-1)+\lambda\,\mathbf 1_{\{m^2:m\ge1\}}(n)\,u(n)$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$, $\mathbb N=\{1,2,\dots\}$, with $u(0)=0$ and $\lambda\ne0$ fixed. Let $\mu$ be the spectral measure of $\delta_1$. Determine the spectral type of $\mu|_{(-2,2)}$; conjecturally it is pure point. (Known: $\mu_{ac}=0$ by Remling's theorem, since every right limit is a single bump, which is not reflectionless.)
why: Sparse potentials with super-geometric gaps (x_{n+1}/x_n -> infinity) are a standard source of singular continuous spectrum (Pearson, Kiselev–Last–Simon). Polynomially sparse spikes are the untouched regime between those and periodic or random potentials. Taking the transfer matrices from one spike to the next turns this operator into a quasi-periodic SL(2,R) cocycle with rotation 2k, where E = 2 cos k. So the frequency of the cocycle depends on the energy, and the existing localization machinery does not apply directly. Cheon–Exner–Šeba conjectured singular continuous spectrum for the continuum analogue, whereas positive Lyapunov exponents point to localization. Deciding which is right tests the methods in a new way.
issues: I defined the Laplacian convention, the boundary condition and the spectral measure. I changed 'prove pure point' to 'determine the spectral type', with pure point as the conjecture, because the answer is not certain. Attack: with E=2cos k, the spike-to-spike cocycle is C·diag(e^{ik(2n+1)},e^{-ik(2n+1)}) with a fixed matrix C. Herman's subharmonicity bound gives a Lyapunov exponent (per spike) of at least log sqrt(1+λ²/(4 sin²k)). Numerics with λ=1 and 20000 spikes match this bound to 3 digits at E=0.3, -1.3, 1.7, 0.05, and give exponent 0 at E=1, where k/π is rational. So generalized eigenfunctions should decay like exp(-γ√x), which is square-summable. Two things stand in the way of a proof: the frequency is tied to the energy, and the phase is fixed at k = ω/2, which is a reflection-symmetric phase. Gordon-type arguments rule out eigenvalues at Liouville k, but that set has measure zero. I found no paper that settles the case x_n=n^2. Kiselev–Last–Simon require x_n/x_{n+1}->0, and Cheon–Exner–Šeba is heuristic and numerical only.

title: Paley spin glass
W: Place a ±1 spin at each element of F_p, and let each pair interact through the Legendre symbol of their difference. Equivalently, this is the max-cut problem for the Paley graph. The eigenvalue bound caps the ground-state energy at p^{3/2}/2. Simple square-wave configurations reach this bound along special primes, but heuristic search for typical primes stalls around 0.46. Is the eigenvalue bound asymptotically sharp for all primes?
M: For primes $p\equiv1\pmod4$ let $E_p=\max_{\sigma\in\{\pm1\}^{\mathbb F_p}}\sum_{i<j}\left(\frac{j-i}{p}\right)\sigma_i\sigma_j$. The matrix $Q=\big(\big(\frac{j-i}p\big)\big)$ has eigenvalues $\pm\sqrt p$ (and $0$), so $E_p\le\frac12p^{3/2}$, and up to $O(p)$ terms $2E_p$ equals the max-cut surplus of the Paley graph. Moreover $\limsup_p E_p/p^{3/2}=\frac12$: if $(\frac qp)=1$ for all primes $q\le y$, then $\sigma_x=\operatorname{sgn}\cos(2\pi x/p)$ has ratio $\frac12-o_y(1)$. Determine $\liminf_{p}E_p/p^{3/2}$; in particular, is it $\frac12$?
why: The question is whether the spectral (Hoffman/Alon) bound for max-cut is asymptotically attained by the most classical quasirandom graph. For random graphs this bound is tight only up to a constant factor. In Fourier terms it asks for ±1 sequences on Z/p whose spectral mass lies almost entirely on the quadratic residues. That makes it an arithmetic question about how the Legendre symbol behaves on small integers, with a Liouville-function-like obstruction at primes where χ(q)=-1 for every small prime q.
issues: Q is symmetric because p≡1 mod 4, so the bound is correct. Attack: with Fourier weights, ratio = Σ_a |σ̂(a)|² χ(a)/(2p²). A square wave dilated by any a gives ratio (4/π²)·Σ_{m odd} χ(m)/m², which tends to 1/2 along primes with χ(q)=1 for all small q. Check: p=53881, where χ(q)=1 for every prime q≤19, gives ratio 0.4925. So limsup=1/2 is easy, and I rewrote the question to ask for the liminf, which is the real content. Simulated annealing gave 0.461, 0.463, 0.464 for p=101, 197, 401, compared with 0.37–0.39 for the best square waves. I found no literature determining the Paley max-cut constant. Recent work on cut surplus versus smallest eigenvalue (arXiv 2509.03490) proves surplus ≤ |λ_min|n/4 but does not treat Paley graphs.

title: Finding Huang's vertex
W: Huang's theorem says that any set of more than half the corners of the n-cube contains a corner with at least √n neighbours in the set. When the set is listed by a small circuit, how hard is it to find such a corner, or a flaw in the listing? The problem is easily shown to be at least as hard as the pigeonhole class PPP. Is it in PPP, so that it is PPP-complete, or does Huang's linear-algebra proof make it harder?
M: $\mathrm{HUANG}$: given a Boolean circuit $f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}^n$, with inputs read as elements of $[2^{n-1}+1]$ and inputs beyond $2^{n-1}+1$ ignored, output either $i\ne j$ with $f(i)=f(j)$, or $i,j_1,\dots,j_m$ with $m=\lceil\sqrt n\rceil$ such that $f(j_1),\dots,f(j_m)$ are distinct and each is at Hamming distance $1$ from $f(i)$. By Huang's theorem this problem is total. It is PPP-hard: embed a PIGEON instance so that every image has even weight, which forces every solution to be a collision. Is $\mathrm{HUANG}\in\mathrm{PPP}$? If not, which standard TFNP class (for example one defined by a linear-algebra principle) contains it, and is it complete for that class?
why: Huang's proof of the sensitivity conjecture is purely spectral, and no combinatorial proof is known. Placing the associated search problem in PPP would amount to a pigeonhole-style, efficiently checkable version of the argument. Showing it lies outside PPP in the black-box model would separate the theorem from counting principles. It is a natural test case for the recent programme of classifying TFNP problems that come from extremal combinatorics (Ramsey, iterated pigeonhole, linear-algebra classes).
issues: My attack: HUANG is PPP-hard. Pad a PIGEON instance with 2^m pigeons and 2^m-1 holes to 2^{n-1}+1 pigeons and 2^{n-1} holes (n-1=m+1, dummy pigeons mapped injectively to dummy holes), and send the holes to even-weight strings. The image then has no cube edges, so every solution is a collision. So 'Is HUANG in FP?' is answered (no, unless PPP is in FP). The question is really about membership in PPP, and I rewrote M around that. Containment in PPA or PLS would put PPP inside those classes, which is unlikely. I found no paper on the TFNP complexity of Huang's theorem. Laplante–Naserasr–Sunny–Wang (2026) give a linear-dependence proof, which may suggest a linear-algebra class.

title: Frozen vortices for Kuramoto on a cube
W: Identical Kuramoto oscillators sit on the grid of a cube's surface. Besides full synchrony, there is a 'longitude' state with a vortex at the centre of the top face and an antivortex at the centre of the bottom face. Prove that this state is a linearly stable equilibrium for every grid size.
M: Let $Q_n$ be the vertex–edge graph of the $n\times n$ subdivided surface of the cube, and $\dot\theta_i=\sum_{j\sim i}\sin(\theta_j-\theta_i)$. Prove that for every odd $n\ge3$ there is an equilibrium $\theta^*$ with the cube's 4-fold rotational symmetry about the vertical axis and winding number $\pm1$ around the central plaquettes of the top and bottom faces, whose Jacobian (the Laplacian with edge weights $\cos(\theta^*_j-\theta^*_i)$) has kernel exactly $\mathrm{span}(\mathbf 1)$ and is otherwise positive. (More generally: for which $n$ does $Q_n$ have a stable non-synchronous equilibrium?)
why: On graphs that triangulate or quadrangulate a sphere there are no twisted states, so any stable non-synchronous state must come from discrete vortices pinned by the lattice. Most known stability criteria need every phase difference below π/2, and this state violates that: by symmetry the central-plaquette edges sit at exactly π/2. So it is a small test case for stability beyond that regime.
issues: The answer appears to be easy and affirmative. Gradient flow from the longitude phase arctan2(y,x) converges for n=3,5,7,9,11 to a symmetric vortex–antivortex equilibrium with synchrony order parameter 0. Its weighted Laplacian has a simple zero eigenvalue, and the next eigenvalue is 0.238, 0.128, 0.074, 0.047, 0.032. Stability therefore holds already at n=3, not only for 'large n'. The minimum edge cosine is about 0, because the central-plaquette edges have phase difference exactly π/2, which is why the usual Delabays–Coletta–Jacquod style criteria (all differences below π/2) do not apply directly. I made the statement concrete: odd n, symmetric vortex state, and linear stability modulo the global rotation.

title: How nearly can tetrahedra close up
W: A chain of regular tetrahedra glued face to face can never close up exactly (Świerczkowski). How fast can near-misses improve as the chain grows? Simple arguments show the best gap shrinks at least like 3^{-n/12} and at most like 3^{-n}. A counting heuristic predicts exactly 3^{-n/6}.
M: Let $T_0$ be a regular tetrahedron with edge $2\sqrt2$. A chain of length $n$ is $T_0,\dots,T_n$, where $T_{k+1}$ is the reflection of $T_k$ in a face of $T_k$, and that face is not the one shared with $T_{k-1}$. Let $g(n)=\min_{\text{chains}}d_H(T_n,T_0)$ (always positive). Known or easy: $g(n)\ge c\,3^{-n}$, because all vertices lie in $3^{-n}\mathbb Z^3$ when $T_0$ has vertices $(\pm1,\pm1,\pm1)$ with an even number of minus signs. A pigeonhole argument on pairs of half-length chains gives $\liminf\frac1n\log g(n)\le-\frac{\log3}{12}$ along suitable $n$. Determine $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log g(n)$ (or the liminf), conjecturally $-\frac{\log 3}{6}$.
why: Steinhaus's tetrahedral-chain problem asks whether a ring can close. It is a concrete free-product subgroup of the isometry group with all entries in Z[1/3]. The rotation parts behave like the Lubotzky–Phillips–Sarnak quaternions of norm 3^n. The near-closure rate is therefore an optimal-approximation question in an S-arithmetic group acting on R^3, combining a Ramanujan-type rotation part with a translation part that behaves like a random walk.
issues: I added the trivial bounds so that the problem has a definite target. I also made 'the exact rate' a conjecture: proving equality with log3/6 needs equidistribution of translations at scale 3^{-n/6} together with a matching Diophantine lower bound, which is probably far out of reach. A realistic target is to improve either bound. The original said the minimum is over chains 'of length n' without fixing the edge length, so I fixed coordinates. Numerics up to n=13 (531441 chains) give best distances of about 0.28–0.34. At these lengths translational spread still dominates, so the data say nothing about the exponent. Literature: my web-search budget ran out before I could search this item. I know of Świerczkowski's non-closure theorem and the Elgersma–Wagon work on near-closing tetrahedral rings from memory only, so a check is still needed for any prior statement of this rate.

title: Logic of random Latin squares
W: Pick a Latin square of order n uniformly at random and read it as a multiplication table x∘y on n symbols. Does every first-order statement about this structure have a limiting probability as n grows? A zero-one law fails. For example, the number of idempotents x∘x=x should be asymptotically Poisson(1), so the chance that one exists should tend to 1-1/e.
M: Let $L_n$ be a uniformly random Latin square on $[n]$ and $\mathcal Q_n=([n],\circ)$ with $x\circ y=L_n(x,y)$. Prove or disprove the first-order convergence law: for every first-order sentence $\varphi$ in the language $\{\circ\}$ (binary function symbol, with equality), $\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr[\mathcal Q_n\models\varphi]$ exists. A natural first step: $|\{x:x\circ x=x\}|\to\mathrm{Poisson}(1)$ in distribution, so $\Pr[\exists x\,(x\circ x=x)]\to1-e^{-1}$. More generally, for every fixed finite partial quasigroup configuration, the count of copies with bounded expectation should have a Poisson limit.
why: Zero-one and convergence laws are known for random graphs, random unary functions (Lynch) and sparse random graphs. Random Latin squares are a natural dense algebraic model with heavy global constraints, where independence-based methods fail. Recent progress on the structure of random Latin squares (Kwan–Sah–Sawhney–Simkin and others) makes a logical limit law a plausible but nontrivial target. It would show which finite configurations the first-order theory can 'see'.
issues: The question is well posed. Definable sparse relations, such as the diagonal map x↦x∘x or the relation x∘y=y, behave like random functions or permutations with Poisson statistics, so the 'first step' captures the expected mechanism. I made the language and the reading of the structure explicit. I could not finish the literature check because the web-search budget ran out. I believe results on Poisson limits for small substructures of random Latin squares may already exist (possibly including idempotents on the diagonal), so the 'first step' may be known. I found no reference posing the convergence-law question itself, but that is unverified.

title: KdV with a cosine coefficient
W: Put a cos x in front of the cubic term of the modified KdV equation on the circle. The energy and the mean are still conserved, but the L² norm is not, and the energy no longer has a definite sign. Can smooth solutions blow up in finite time?
M: Consider $u_t+u_{xxx}+(\cos(x)\,u^3)_x=0$ on $\mathbb T=\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$ with real $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb T)$. It is Hamiltonian, $u_t=\partial_x\frac{\delta H}{\delta u}$ with $H=\int(\tfrac12u_x^2-\tfrac14\cos(x)u^4)$, and conserves $\int u$ and $H$. However, $\frac{d}{dt}\int u^2=\frac12\int\sin(x)u^4$. Decide whether every such $u_0$ yields a global smooth solution, or whether $\|u(t)\|_{H^1}\to\infty$ in finite time for some $u_0$.
why: Standard mKdV on the torus is globally well-posed because L² conservation and the L²-subcritical Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequality control the energy. A spatially varying coefficient breaks the translation symmetry and so the L² law, which removes the a priori bound. Any blow-up would have to come from L² growth rather than L² concentration. That is a mechanism of real interest for inhomogeneous dispersive equations, and this is about the simplest model where it could occur.
issues: I checked the conservation laws: ∫u is a Casimir and H is the Hamiltonian, while d/dt||u||² = (1/2)∫ sin x u⁴, so L² can grow. The a priori estimates close only into dM/dt ≲ M³, which does not rule out blow-up. The weighted mass ∫|cos x|^{1/3}u² cancels the quartic term in the Kato identity, but that weight is singular at the zeros of cos, so it gives no global bound. Numerics (Fourier, N=512, integrating-factor RK4, dt=1e-5, initial data 3exp(-4(x-π/2)²)) conserve H=11.28 to 4 digits while ||u||² grows from 6.4 to 12.7 by t=0.8. The coarser run dt=2e-5 reached 23.9 at t=1.0 and then lost resolution. That growth is consistent with blow-up but does not establish it. Cos x is one arbitrary choice, and the same question makes sense for any sign-changing smooth coefficient a(x). I could not finish the literature check because the web-search budget ran out; work on inhomogeneous gKdV exists, but I could not check whether this case is covered.

title: Real-rank hyperoperation uniqueness
W: Find natural rules that single out exactly one way to fill in operations between addition, multiplication and exponentiation, and prove exactly one family obeys them.
M: Let $a>1$ and $F_s(b)=a[s]b$ for $s\in[1,3]$, $b>0$, with $F_1(b)=a+b$, $F_2(b)=ab$, $F_3(b)=a^b$ and $F_{s+1}(b+1)=F_s(F_{s+1}(b))$ for $s\in[1,2]$. Find natural extra conditions (analyticity in $(s,b)$ plus a convexity condition in $s$) under which exactly one such family exists, and prove it.
why: Interpolating integer-indexed operations to real rank is a well-known folklore problem. A Bohr–Mollerup-type uniqueness theorem would settle it the way log-convexity settles the Gamma function.
issues: As submitted, M is not a precise statement: it does not say what the recursion law is, what log-convexity means, or what is log-convex. The recursion also only makes sense for s in [1,2]. Given F_s on [1,2], F_{s+1} is a fractional iterate of F_s, so it is fixed only up to the choice of fractional iteration. The whole of [1,2] is then a free family between a+b and ab, and one scalar convexity condition cannot plausibly pin it down. Finding the right axioms is the open problem itself, not a gap in the wording. Ill-posed as stated; the repaired M above is a research programme, not a definite question.

title: Hearing tetrahedra
W: Triangles can be heard: their Dirichlet spectrum determines them up to congruence (Durso 1988; Grieser–Maronna 2013). Show the same for tetrahedra.
M: Let $T_1,T_2\subset\mathbb R^3$ be (nondegenerate) tetrahedra whose Dirichlet Laplacian eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, coincide. Prove that $T_1$ and $T_2$ are congruent.
why: This is the natural next case of Kac's question after triangles. The heat-trace invariants of a polyhedron (volume, surface area, an edge sum weighted by dihedral angles, vertex terms) give about four numbers, but a tetrahedron has six degrees of freedom, so a proof would need new input from the wave trace or periodic billiard orbits in 3D polyhedra. It would be the first 'hearable' class of 3D polyhedra with more than a few parameters.
issues: Tried the heat-invariant count: 4 invariants against 6 parameters, so the heat trace cannot be enough; the problem is not trivial. Found no proof and no isospectral counterexample. The surveys found (Grieser–Maronna, Rowlett et al.) state the polygon/triangle results and do not list tetrahedra as solved. Likely a known folklore question, so novelty is low. Added 'with multiplicity'.

title: Sup norms on the Fermat quartic
W: On a round sphere, some eigenfunctions pile up at the poles as much as is possible. Show this cannot happen on the surface x⁴+y⁴+z⁴=1.
M: Let $S=\{x^4+y^4+z^4=1\}\subset\mathbb R^3$ with the induced metric, and let $\Delta\varphi=-\lambda\varphi$, $\|\varphi\|_{L^2(S)}=1$. Prove $\sup_{\varphi}\|\varphi\|_{L^\infty(S)}=o(\lambda^{1/4})$ as $\lambda\to\infty$. Equivalently (Sogge–Zelditch), prove that $S$ has no pole: no point $p$ such that every geodesic from $p$ comes back to $p$ as a smoothly closed geodesic.
why: Sogge–Zelditch showed that a real-analytic surface has maximal eigenfunction growth only if it has a pole. Proving that explicit surfaces have no pole is the missing step for concrete examples; the triaxial ellipsoid is already done.
issues: By Sogge–Zelditch II (arXiv 1409.2063), S is real-analytic, so the problem reduces exactly to showing S has no pole. That is a purely dynamical question about geodesics, probably checkable by rigorous numerics plus symmetry. The choice of surface is arbitrary; it is a second instance of a method already used for ellipsoids. Clarified the eigenvalue convention: λ^{1/4} with λ the eigenvalue is the sharp exponent.

title: Is the Petersen graph common?
W: Color the edges of a huge complete graph red and blue. Does a random coloring minimize the number of single-color copies of the Petersen graph?
M: Let $P$ be the Petersen graph ($10$ vertices, $15$ edges) and $m(P)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\min_{\chi}\frac{\#\{\text{monochromatic copies of }P\text{ in }(K_n,\chi)\}}{\#\{\text{copies of }P\text{ in }K_n\}}$, minimum over red/blue colorings $\chi$ of $E(K_n)$. Is $m(P)=2^{-14}$, i.e. is $P$ common? Equivalently, is $t(P,W)+t(P,1-W)\ge 2^{-14}$ for every graphon $W$? If not, determine $m(P)$.
why: Which graphs are common (random coloring is optimal) is a central question in Ramsey multiplicity. The known obstructions (containing $K_4$, the Turán-coloring criterion of Fox–Wigderson) do not apply to the triangle-free, girth-5, 3-chromatic Petersen graph. It is a natural test case, between odd cycles (common) and graphs containing $K_4$ (uncommon).
issues: Original 'determine the constant' rewritten as the commonness question; if P is common the constant is 2^{-14}. Checks: P has no K4, so Thomason's obstruction does not apply. Its smallest even subgraph with min degree 2 is C6, and t(C6,U)>=0, so P passes the first local-commonness test. Turán colorings give 32-560 times the random value. A random search over 2- to 4-step graphons found nothing below 2^{-14} (best 1.035x). Found no paper settling P.

title: Is the measure of the hyperbolic real quadratic parameters computable?
W: For real c between −2 and 1/4, the map x ↦ x²+c has an attracting cycle for an open dense set of c, yet the chaotic parameters have positive length (Jakobson). Is the total length of the parameters with an attracting cycle a computable number? It can be approximated from below by listing windows, but no known method approximates it from above.
M: Let $H=\{c\in[-2,1/4]:\ x\mapsto x^2+c\text{ has an attracting periodic orbit}\}$. Is the Lebesgue measure $\lambda(H)$ a computable real number? ($H$ is open and its components can be certified by interval arithmetic, so $\lambda(H)$ is lower semicomputable; Jakobson's theorem gives $\lambda(H)<9/4$.) Equivalently: is the measure of the set of stochastic (Collet–Eckmann) parameters lower semicomputable?
why: This is a basic constant of one-dimensional dynamics, and no rigorous nontrivial upper bound on it is known. Computer-assisted Jakobson-type schemes (Luzzatto–Takahashi; Golmakani–Koudjinan–Luzzatto–Pilarczyk) certify expansion, not stochasticity. A positive answer would give a certified two-sided estimate; a negative one would be a striking non-computability result for a natural dynamical quantity.
issues: Checked the reduction: the stochastic set is a countable union over CE constants of intersections of finite-time conditions. That makes each piece upper semicomputable, which is the wrong direction, so the answer does not follow from the obvious approach. Golmakani et al. (2020) certify an escape-time property on about 90% of a parameter piece but explicitly do not prove stochasticity. Found no paper on computability of λ(H). Statement is precise (parabolic parameters have measure zero).

title: Integrability of the egg-crate torus
W: Put the surface z = ε sin x sin y over a flat square torus. Show its geodesic flow is never integrable, however small the bumps are.
M: For $\varepsilon>0$ let $g_\varepsilon$ be the metric on $\mathbb T^2=\mathbb R^2/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^2$ induced from the graph $z=\varepsilon\sin x\sin y$, i.e. $g_\varepsilon=dx^2+dy^2+\varepsilon^2(\cos x\sin y\,dx+\sin x\cos y\,dy)^2$. Prove that for every $\varepsilon>0$ the geodesic flow on $T^*\mathbb T^2\setminus0$ has no real-analytic first integral functionally independent of the Hamiltonian (for example, by showing positive topological entropy).
why: Kozlov's theorem rules out first integrals that are analytic in ε for generic trigonometric perturbations of the flat torus. Proving non-integrability at each fixed ε, uniformly down to ε→0, needs control of exponentially small splitting at resonances. This is an explicit test of that gap.
issues: Wrote out the metric explicitly. The ε-analytic (Poincaré–Kozlov) version follows from Kozlov because the Fourier spectrum of the perturbation is not on a line. The fixed-ε statement for all ε>0 seems open but is quite specific. By Paternain/Taimanov, positive topological entropy would be enough.

title: Icosahedral monotile
W: Find a single 3D tile that fills space and forces five-fold, icosahedral symmetry in every tiling, or prove that no such tile exists.
M: Does there exist a compact set $T\subset\mathbb R^3$ homeomorphic to a ball, which tiles $\mathbb R^3$ by congruent copies, such that for every tiling $\mathcal T$ by copies of $T$ the hull $\Omega(\mathcal T)=\overline{\{\mathcal T+x:x\in\mathbb R^3\}}$ (local topology) satisfies $R\,\Omega(\mathcal T)=\Omega(\mathcal T)$ for every $R$ in some icosahedral rotation group $G\cong A_5$? (This forces strong aperiodicity, by the crystallographic restriction.)
why: Icosahedral quasicrystals are modeled by tilings with two or more prototiles (Ammann rhombohedra, Danzer tetrahedra). The new 3D aperiodic monotiles, such as Socolar–Taylor and recent strongly aperiodic examples, all live in crystallographic orientation classes. A single tile that forces non-crystallographic symmetry would close that gap.
issues: Made precise: 'icosahedral symmetry in its hull' now means hull invariance under an A5 rotation group. Ball topology added to exclude degenerate disconnected tiles. Recent 3D strongly aperiodic monotiles (e.g. arXiv 2609.19214) use cubic frames, with symmetry order at most 24, so they do not answer this. Even the 2D analogue (a monotile forcing 5- or 10-fold symmetry) seems open and is the more natural first target, which keeps this at B.

title: Proof complexity of the sensitivity theorem
W: Huang proved that any set of more than half the corners of the n-cube contains a corner with at least √n neighbours inside the set. Write this as a propositional formula with one variable per corner. Do polynomial-size proofs exist in resolution, cutting planes or sum-of-squares, measured against the 2^n variables?
M: Let $N=2^n$, $d=\lceil\sqrt n\rceil-1$. $\mathrm{SENS}_n$ is the CNF on variables $x_v$ ($v\in\{0,1\}^n$) plus sequential-counter variables encoding $\sum_v x_v\ge 2^{n-1}+1$, together with the clauses $\neg x_v\vee\bigvee_{u\in U}\neg x_u$ for every $v$ and every $(d+1)$-set $U$ of neighbours of $v$ (size $N\cdot n^{O(\sqrt n)}=N^{1+o(1)}$). It is unsatisfiable by Huang's theorem. Does $\mathrm{SENS}_n$ have refutations of size $N^{O(1)}$ in (a) resolution, (b) cutting planes, (c) sum-of-squares of degree $O(\log N)$? Lower bounds $2^{N^{\Omega(1)}}$ are equally of interest.
why: Huang's proof is a short spectral argument, interlacing for a signed adjacency matrix. Asking whether weak proof systems can capture it tests how much linear algebra cutting planes and SOS can simulate. It belongs to the programme of locating famous combinatorial theorems in the proof-complexity hierarchy.
issues: Checked the sizes: the formula has size N^{1+o(1)}, and Huang's bound gives unsatisfiability exactly at d=ceil(sqrt n)-1. Part (a) is probably 'no' for routine pigeonhole/matching reasons: even the d=0 case (an independent set larger than N/2) is a matching-type principle that is hard for resolution. That case is easy in cutting planes via a perfect matching. So (b) and (c) are the real content, and the W wording should stress them. Found no prior work on this.

title: Lane–Emden with a shift
W: Replace u² in the five-dimensional Lane–Emden equation by the square of u at a shifted point. Are there still no positive solutions?
M: Let $e\in\mathbb R^5\setminus\{0\}$. Does there exist a positive $u\in C^2(\mathbb R^5)$ with $-\Delta u(x)=u(x+e)^2$ for all $x\in\mathbb R^5$?
why: For $p<(n+2)/(n-2)$ (here $2<7/3$), Gidas–Spruck shows $-\Delta u=u^p$ has no positive entire solutions. Their proof, like moving planes, relies on the nonlinearity being local, so a shifted nonlinearity tests which Liouville methods survive nonlocal coupling.
issues: 1D analogue is trivially impossible (positive concave on R is constant). The superharmonic-inequality threshold n/(n-2)=5/3<2 does not settle it, and |x|^{-3} decay is not excluded by crude integral estimates. Found no literature on shifted-argument Lane–Emden. The choice of n=5, p=2 is arbitrary; the natural version is 'for all n≥3, 1<p<(n+2)/(n-2)'.

title: Hat Ising universality
W: Magnets on a hat tiling should behave at their critical point exactly like magnets on a square grid. Prove it.
M: Let $G$ be the planar graph whose vertices are the tiles of a fixed hat tiling (Smith–Myers–Kaplan–Goodman-Strauss), with edges between tiles sharing a boundary segment. Consider the ferromagnetic nearest-neighbour Ising model on $G$ with uniform coupling $J=1$. Prove that there is a critical $\beta_c$ (independent of the tiling in the hull), and that as $\beta\to\beta_c$ the spontaneous magnetization, susceptibility and correlation length obey $M(\beta)\asymp(\beta-\beta_c)^{1/8}$, $\chi(\beta)\asymp|\beta-\beta_c|^{-7/4}$, $\xi(\beta)\asymp|\beta-\beta_c|^{-1}$.
why: Rigorous 2D Ising universality is known for isoradial graphs at Z-invariant weights and for periodic graphs. Uniform couplings on an aperiodic, non-isoradial graph are not covered. The hat graph is a canonical such test, and numerics (Matsubara–Suzuki) support universality.
issues: Original M did not say which graph, which couplings, or which definitions of the exponents. Fixed: tile-adjacency graph, uniform J, and asymptotics up to constants. Existing work is Monte Carlo only, with ν and β assumed rather than fitted. This is an instance of the broader open problem of universality for quasiperiodic planar Ising models.

title: Smallest degree of a Keller counterexample in dimension 3
W: In 2026 the Jacobian conjecture was refuted in three variables. The first explicit counterexample (Alpöge's map) has polynomial degree 7. Wang's theorem says degree 2 is impossible. What is the smallest degree a counterexample in three variables can have? In particular, is there one of degree 3, 4 or 5?
M: Let $d_3$ be the least $d$ such that some polynomial map $F:\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^3$ with $\max_i\deg F_i=d$ and $\det DF\in\mathbb C^\times$ is not an automorphism. Wang's theorem gives $d_3\ge3$, and Alpöge's map gives $d_3\le7$. Determine $d_3$. In particular, decide whether $d_3\le5$.
why: Once the conjecture is false in dimension 3, the main remaining question is how much room counterexamples need. Wang's quadratic theorem and the Bass–Connell–Wright cubic-homogeneous reduction both point to low degree as the decisive regime. Settling $d_3$ means either proving the conjecture for all cubic, quartic or quintic maps in three variables, which would be new even for cubics, or finding a much smaller counterexample. The answer tells us whether the phenomenon is rigid or flexible.
issues: The original 'degree 5 or less' was arbitrary, so I recast it as determining the minimal degree $d_3\in[3,7]$ and kept the $\le5$ question as the special case. Known facts: Alpöge's map (degrees 7,6,4; Jacobian -2; generically 3-to-1), a second map G (degrees 4,11,12), and Gallagher's family of every geometric degree $\ge3$ (polynomial degrees not stated in the sources I read). Wang excludes degree 2. 'Degree' must mean polynomial degree, not geometric/fibre degree, because the 2026 papers use both. The general (nonhomogeneous) cubic case in dimension 3 does not appear to be settled in the literature I found. Section 8 of arXiv:2607.20210 shows that for fixed bounded degrees, existence over an algebraically closed field is decidable by elimination. So small cases may be attackable by computation, which is a risk that this gets settled quickly. Wright's cubic-homogeneous result in dimension 3 is recalled from memory and was not re-checked. I found no source that poses the minimal-degree question explicitly.

title: Forced blow-up up to the Lions threshold
W: With an ordinary Laplacian, a smooth compactly supported push can make a fluid at rest blow up in finite time (OpenAI, 2026). With dissipation (-Δ)^α for α ≥ 5/4, Lions proved that solutions stay smooth. Does forced blow-up from rest still happen for every α strictly between 1 and 5/4?
M:
For $\alpha\in(1,5/4)$ consider $\partial_tu+(u\cdot
abla)u+
abla p=-(-\Delta)^{\alpha}u+f$, $
abla\cdot u=0$ on $\mathbb R^3$, $u(\cdot,0)=0$. Decide whether for every such $\alpha$ there is $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3	imes(0,\infty);\mathbb R^3)$ for which the smooth solution breaks down in finite time, i.e. $\limsup_{t\uparrow T}\|u(t)\|_{L^\infty}=\infty$ for some $T<\infty$.
why: Lions' threshold $\alpha=5/4$ is exactly where energy-level dissipation becomes critical, so it is the natural candidate for the sharp boundary between regularity and singularity. The 2026 construction of forced blow-up at $\alpha=1$ makes the forced form of this question meaningful. Pushing it to every $\alpha<5/4$ would show that the energy-critical exponent is the true dividing line, at least when forcing is allowed.
issues: As written the range '$\alpha<5/4$' included $\alpha=1$, which is a form of Clay's forced statement and was claimed in 2026 by OpenAI. That paper proves smooth, compactly supported, time-dependent force, zero data, all $\nu>0$, not yet refereed. Cao–Chi–Nie use it as a black box. I restricted to $\alpha\in(1,5/4)$ and changed 'construct' to 'decide'. Hypodissipative forced blow-up is known for $\alpha<\alpha_0\approx0.093$ with a rougher force (arXiv:2407.06776). None of the sources treat $\alpha>1$ or mention Lions' threshold. Breakdown is defined via $L^\infty$.

title: Blow-up under a steady force
W: The 2026 forced Navier–Stokes blow-up uses a push that varies in time and is switched on and off. Can a smooth, compactly supported push that never changes in time also drive a fluid at rest to a singularity?
M:
Decide whether there is $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, independent of $t$, such that the solution of $\partial_tu+(u\cdot
abla)u+
abla p=\Delta u+f$, $
abla\cdot u=0$, $u(\cdot,0)=0$ on $\mathbb R^3$ loses smoothness in finite time.
why: Steady stirring is the physically basic forcing, and a time-independent force cannot be tuned to the scales of a developing singularity. A positive answer would mean the singularity is produced by the nonlinearity alone under a fixed energy input. A negative answer would show that the time-dependent forcing in known constructions is essential.
issues: Before 2026 this was a strengthening of Clay's forced statement. After OpenAI's claimed time-dependent forced blow-up (force supported away from $t=0$, not yet refereed) it is the natural next step. Only gradient forces are excluded trivially, since they give the zero solution (Cao–Chi–Nie Prop. 3.17), so $f$ must have a nontrivial solenoidal part. Heuristic: a bounded steady force is subcritical at small scales, so near the singular point the blow-up is essentially unforced. This is probably far harder than the time-dependent case and close to Millennium level, which limits its value as a list item. I changed the wording to 'decide'.

title: Prime-sum labelling of balanced trees
W: (As stated, false.) Label a tree with 1 to n so every edge sum is prime. The fixable version: does balance plus bounded maximum degree suffice for large n?
M: (Corrected, grade C.) Fix $\Delta\ge3$. Is there $n_0(\Delta)$ such that every tree on $n\ge n_0$ vertices with maximum degree $\le\Delta$ and bipartition classes of sizes $\lceil n/2\rceil,\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ admits a bijection $V\to[n]$ with every edge sum prime?
why: It extends the classical prime-circle and prime-path arrangements of $1,\dots,n$ (Greenfield–Greenwood) from paths to trees. It mixes the distribution of primes in short intervals with tree embedding.
issues: FALSE as stated. Take a vertex v adjacent to all of the other class (a caterpillar: v joined to all $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ vertices of class B, the remaining A-vertices hung off one B-vertex). This tree is balanced, but v's label a would need a+b prime for every b of the opposite parity in [n], which is impossible once n is moderately large. More generally deg(v) is at most the number of primes in (a,a+n], about n/log n. Brute force over all balanced trees: failures at n=7..14 number 2,3,7,6,12,9,53,64 (n=14: 64 of 895). Every failing tree had max degree $\ge4$, and all balanced trees with $\Delta\le3$ up to n=14 were labellable. The bounded-degree repair is plausible but narrow, grade C at best.

title: Information-tight sorting of pattern classes
W: An array is promised to avoid a fixed pattern. Counting the allowed orders gives a lower bound on the comparisons needed to sort it, and Fredman's theorem says this bound plus 2n always suffices. Opler (2024) showed the right order of magnitude is linear. Is the counting bound tight up to lower-order terms, o(n), for every pattern?
M: For a permutation $\tau$ let $C_\tau(n)$ be the minimum worst-case number of comparisons of a decision tree that sorts $a_1,\dots,a_n$ under the promise that their order pattern lies in $\mathrm{Av}_n(\tau)$. Fredman: $\log_2|\mathrm{Av}_n(\tau)|\le C_\tau(n)\le\log_2|\mathrm{Av}_n(\tau)|+2n$. Decide whether $C_\tau(n)=\log_2|\mathrm{Av}_n(\tau)|+o(n)$ for every $\tau$, and in particular for $\tau=1324$.
why: The comparison model is one of the few settings where information-theoretic lower bounds are often nearly exact. Even for unrestricted sorting it is unknown whether $\log_2 n!+o(n)$ comparisons suffice. Pattern classes give a family where this question is harder to dismiss. A linear gap for some $\tau$ would need a new lower-bound technique, and tightness for every $\tau$ would need a strong structural sorting algorithm.
issues: Opler (arXiv:2409.07868) gives $O((\log c_\tau+1)n)$, tight up to a constant factor, but not the additive $o(n)$ question. I found nowhere that poses the additive form. Small cases: for $\tau\in\{132,231,312,213\}$ (equivalent under reversal and complement, which preserve the sorting problem; inverse does not), stack sorting uses $\le2n$ comparisons and $\log_2 C_n=2n-O(\log n)$, so the answer is yes. $\tau\in\{123,321\}$ seems tractable by an adaptive merge but I did not check it. The question is substantive only for $|\tau|\ge4$. I stated that the decision tree knows $\tau$.

title: Outer billiards around a superellipse
W: Outer billiards around a smooth convex shape with positive curvature has only bounded orbits (Moser–Douady). Polygons and generic C¹ shapes can have unbounded orbits. Decide what happens for the analytic shape x⁴+y⁴ ≤ 1, whose curvature vanishes at four points.
M: Let $K=\{x^4+y^4\le1\}$ and let $T:\mathbb R^2\setminus K\to\mathbb R^2\setminus K$ be the outer billiard map: $T(p)=2q-p$, where $q\in\partial K$ is the point of tangency of the right-hand tangent line from $p$. Decide whether every $T$-orbit is bounded.
why: Douady's proof needs $C^6$ and positive curvature. At a flat point the inverse Gauss map is only Hölder (the support function here is $C^{1,1/3}$), so the twist map at infinity is not smooth enough for KAM. Unbounded orbits are known for some polygons (Schwartz), semicircles (Dolgopyat–Fayad) and generic $C^1$ symmetric tables. This analytic example tests whether isolated flat points alone can destroy confinement.
issues: I found no treatment of tables with isolated zero-curvature points. The 2026 $C^1$-generic result (arXiv:2610.06418) covers tables whose radius-of-curvature measure is purely singular, which is not this case: here it is absolutely continuous with integrable singularities $\sim|\theta|^{-2/3}$. T is well defined because $K$ is strictly convex. Numerical check: one orbit starting at $\ell^4$-gauge 30.7, run for $1.18\times10^6$ steps, stayed in gauge [21.55, 30.82] with no drift, which is weak evidence for boundedness. The statement is unchanged.

title: Rotation-proof lattice-point-poor shapes
W: Among convex shapes of area A, how few lattice points can a shape be guaranteed to contain under every rotation about the origin? Can any shape do much better than a disc centred at the origin?
M: For $A>0$ let $m(A)=\inf\{\sup_{\theta}\#(\rho_\theta K\cap\mathbb Z^2): K\subset\mathbb R^2\text{ compact convex},\ |K|=A\}$. Decide whether $m(A)\ge A-O_\varepsilon(A^{1/4+\varepsilon})$.
why: It is a rotation-uniform form of the Gauss circle problem. An origin-centred disc is rotation-invariant, and its deficit $A-N(\sqrt{A/\pi})$ can reach order $A^{1/4}$ (Hardy–Landau). The question is whether any convex body does essentially better.
issues: The original 'determine the convex K … to second-order term' is ill-posed. The optimiser depends on A arithmetically. For discs the value is the circle-problem count $N(R)$, which oscillates, so there is no definite second-order term. I replaced it with a definite inequality question. Heuristic: sup over rotations is at least the rotation average $\sum_n r_2(n)\,\theta_K(\sqrt n)/2\pi$, which differs from A by a small smoothed error, so a deficit much larger than $A^{1/4}$ seems unlikely. The problem stays tied to circle-problem exponents and is fairly arbitrary. My searches found no direct literature.

title: Deciding rationality of PL rotation numbers
W: A circle homeomorphism made of finitely many straight pieces, with rational break points and slopes, has a rotation number. Rational rotation numbers can be confirmed by finding a rational periodic orbit. Irrational ones occur too: Belk–Hyde–Moore found √2−1 with slopes 3/2, 2/3, 1. Is there an algorithm that always decides which case holds?
M: Let $\mathcal P$ be the set of orientation-preserving PL homeomorphisms of $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with finitely many rational break points, rational slopes and $f(0)\in\mathbb Q$, encoded by these data. Is $\{f\in\mathcal P:\rho(f)\in\mathbb Q\}$ decidable? (It is computably enumerable: if $\rho(f)=p/q$, the zero set of the lift $F^q(x)-x-p$ is a nonempty finite union of rational points and rational intervals.)
why: Rotation numbers of rational PL maps link Thompson-like groups $T_q$, renormalisation, and number theory. Belk–Hyde–Moore conjecture that the irrational values are quadratic when slopes are powers of one rational, and they ask about decidability for one-parameter families and for finite order in $T_q$. A decision procedure would amount to a structure theorem for when renormalisation of such maps fails to close up.
issues: Belk–Hyde–Moore (arXiv:2211.05825) give an explicit rational map with $\rho=\sqrt2-1$, refuting Calegari's question. Their Questions 3–4 are close relatives (deciding for the family $f_{q,r}$, and finite order in $T_q$) but not this exact question, and I found no paper posing it. The c.e. direction checks out. $\rho$ is computable, which only helps for a fixed candidate $p/q$. The statement is clean; I added the encoding and the c.e. justification.

title: L⁴ Strichartz on the surface of a cube
W: On a square torus, the L⁴ Strichartz estimate for the Schrödinger equation loses only ε derivatives (Bourgain). On general flat surfaces with cone points only a 1/4-derivative loss is known. Decide whether the cube surface, with eight cone points of angle 3π/2 that diffract waves, behaves like the torus.
M: Let $S$ be the surface of the unit cube with its flat metric, and $\Delta$ the Friedrichs extension of the Laplacian from $C_c^\infty(S\setminus\{\text{vertices}\})$. Decide whether for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $C_\varepsilon$ with $\|e^{it\Delta}f\|_{L^4([0,1]\times S)}\le C_\varepsilon\|f\|_{H^\varepsilon(S)}$ for all $f$.
why: The cube surface is an arithmetic surface with cone points. Its 'nonsingular' eigenfunctions lift to trigonometric polynomials (Greif–Kaplan–Strichartz–Wiese), but the singular ones are not explicit, and diffraction at the vertices spoils the lattice-counting proof used on the torus. Blair–Ford–Marzuola obtain a $1/p$ loss on all compact flat cone surfaces and suggest the loss is an artefact of their method. The cube is the simplest test case where arithmetic structure and diffraction compete.
issues: Sources: Blair–Ford–Marzuola Thm 1.5 gives a $H^{1/4}$ bound for p=q=4 on compact Euclidean surfaces with conical singularities, and Remark 1.3 suggests the loss is not sharp. I found no ε-loss result for any surface whose cone angles are not of the form $2\pi/k$; pillowcase-type quotients of tori are easy. I specified the Friedrichs extension and changed 'prove' to 'decide', since the truth is unclear. The estimate would force $\|\varphi\|_{L^4}\lesssim\lambda^{\varepsilon}$ for the singular eigenfunctions and needs near-coincidence counting for an irregular spectrum.

title: Ising spin at a cube corner
W: Glue three quarter-planes of the square grid into the surface of an infinite cube corner (a flat cone of angle 3π/2) and run the critical Ising model. Prove that the spin at the corner decorrelates with the exponent 7/24 predicted by conformal field theory.
M: Let $\Gamma$ be the union of the three quadrant lattices $\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2$ on the faces of $\partial\mathbb R_{\ge0}^3$, glued along the coordinate axes, with apex $o$ (degree 3; every other vertex has degree 4). Let $\langle\cdot\rangle$ be the infinite-volume limit of the nearest-neighbour Ising model at $\beta_c=\tfrac12\log(1+\sqrt2)$ with free boundary conditions on $\Gamma\cap\{\|x\|_\infty\le n\}$. Prove $\langle\sigma_o\sigma_x\rangle\asymp|x|^{-7/24}$ as $|x|\to\infty$.
why: Rigorous conformal invariance of Ising spin correlations (Chelkak–Hongler–Izyurov) is proved for planar domains, and a conical point is the simplest source of curvature. Under $w=z^{4/3}$ the apex spin acquires scaling dimension $\tfrac{2\pi}{\alpha}\cdot\tfrac18=\tfrac16$, so the two-point exponent is $\tfrac16+\tfrac18=\tfrac7{24}$. This exponent depends on the geometry and differs from both the bulk value $1/4$ and the corner values. Proving it would extend discrete complex analysis to cone singularities.
issues: I checked the CFT computation: $|w|^{-1/4}|w'(x)|^{1/8}$ with $w=z^{4/3}$ gives $|x|^{-1/3+1/24}=|x|^{-7/24}$. Physics papers confirm CFT predictions numerically for conical lattices (Costa-Santos, free-energy log terms), but I found no rigorous spin-exponent result on cones. Chelkak–Izyurov–Mahfouf (arXiv:2104.12858) and CHI cover only planar or isoradial planar settings. I specified β_c and the infinite-volume measure, which were missing, and noted that the gluing is a locally flat square lattice away from $o$. Risk: this may be within reach of existing spinor and s-holomorphic methods.

title: Three-pile shuffle group
W: Using the six ways to stack three piles in a perfect shuffle, which rearrangements of the deck can you reach? (Already answered.)
M: Determine $G_{3,3n}=\langle \rho_\tau\sigma:\tau\in S_3\rangle\le S_{3n}$. Known answer: $G_{3,3^m}=S_3\wr C_m$; for $n$ not a power of $3$, $G_{3,3n}=S_{3n}$ if $n\not\equiv0\pmod 4$ and $A_{3n}$ if $n\equiv0\pmod4$.
why: Generalises the Diaconis-Graham-Kantor determination of the two-pile perfect-shuffle group; it is the k=3 case of the Medvedoff-Morrison shuffle group conjecture.
issues: Fully solved. Xia-Zhang-Zhang-Zhu (arXiv 2304.01037, Forum Math. Sigma 2024) prove the Medvedoff-Morrison conjecture for all k and give the exact group for k=3 (Thm 1.5): S_3 wr C_m when 3n=3^m, else S_{3n} or A_{3n} by n mod 4. The power-of-k case is due to Medvedoff-Morrison (1987) and Amarra-Morgan-Praeger (arXiv 1908.05128).

title: Monotile assembly threshold
W: (Corrected, already posed.) For tiling simply connected regions with a fixed set of rectangles, two rectangles give a polynomial-time problem while a large set is NP-complete. Do three rectangles suffice for NP-completeness?
M: (Pak-Yang Conjecture 7.5.) Prove there is a set $T$ of three rectangles such that deciding whether a finite simply connected region of $\mathbb Z^2$ can be tiled by translates of tiles from $T$ is NP-complete. (Remila: every two-rectangle set gives a polynomial-time problem.)
why: Locates the exact point where local tiling constraints become computationally universal. It ties tiling theory to the size of the smallest gadgets that can encode SAT.
issues: As stated, the problem is answered or ill-posed. With holes allowed, a single tile (the right tromino) is already NP-complete (Moore-Robson 2001), so t=1, and the 'fewer polygons give P' part is then vacuous. Also, 'NP-complete vs polynomial' is only a dichotomy if P!=NP is assumed. The natural fix (simply connected regions, rectangles) is Pak-Yang's stated Conjecture 7.5 (3 rectangles), so it is not novel. Best known bounds are 111 rectangles / 23 Wang tiles (arXiv 2405.01017) against the lower bound of 3 (Remila).

title: Largest prime factor of Markov numbers
W: Markov numbers are the numbers appearing in positive integer solutions of x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz. Show that the largest prime factor of a Markov number tends to infinity. Equivalently, for any finite set of primes, only finitely many Markov numbers are built from those primes alone.
M: Let $\mathcal M=\{m\ge1:\exists\,x,y\in\mathbb Z_{>0},\ x^2+y^2+m^2=3xym\}$ and let $P(m)$ denote the largest prime factor of $m$ (with $P(1)=1$). Prove that $P(m)\to\infty$ as $m\to\infty$ in $\mathcal M$; equivalently, for every finite set $S$ of primes, only finitely many $m\in\mathcal M$ are $S$-units.
why: Corvaja and Zannier used the Subspace Theorem to show that the greatest prime factor of the product xy over Markov pairs tends to infinity. The single-number version is the natural strengthening. It sits next to the uniqueness conjecture, where Markov numbers that are prime powers are already handled, and to recent strong-approximation work on the Markoff surface.
issues: I found no proof. Single branches are easy: for example, the branch of odd-indexed Fibonacci numbers follows from primitive-divisor theorems. The difficulty is uniformity over the whole tree. Counting does not decide it: there are about (log X)^2 Markov numbers up to X but (log X)^{|S|} S-units, so counting rules out nothing once |S|>=2. A computer check of the 576 Markov numbers up to 1e24 found nothing surprising (smallest largest prime factors above 1000: 53, 61, 109, ...). I did not confirm whether Corvaja-Zannier state the single-number case as open, so novelty is uncertain. The M was made explicit (definition of the set, convention P(1)=1).

title: Ringel for forests
W: Ringel's conjecture, now a theorem for large n, says the complete graph on 2m+1 vertices splits into 2m+1 copies of any tree with m edges. Show the same holds for every forest with m edges. A stronger form asks that every such forest have a rho-labelling, which gives a cyclic decomposition.
M: Prove that for every $m\ge1$ and every forest $F$ with $m$ edges, $E(K_{2m+1})$ can be partitioned into $2m+1$ subgraphs each isomorphic to $F$. Stronger form: every such $F$ admits an injective map $f:V(F)\to\mathbb Z_{2m+1}$ whose edge lengths $\min(|f(u)-f(v)|,\,2m+1-|f(u)-f(v)|)$ are exactly $1,\dots,m$ (a $\rho$-labelling).
why: Montgomery-Pokrovskiy-Sudakov and Keevash-Staden proved Ringel's conjecture for large trees. Their rainbow-copy and cyclic-shift framework does not need connectivity, but the embedding steps do. So the question is whether connectivity is essential to Ringel-type decompositions. A positive answer would be a natural forest analogue of the Kotzig-Ringel-Rosa theorem.
issues: No counterexample found. A backtracking search found rho-labellings (and hence cyclic decompositions of K_{2m+1}) for all forests without isolated vertices with m<=9 edges (2, 4, 8, 16, 34, 71, 154, 341 forests). I found no paper stating or proving the forest version: MPS, Keevash-Staden and the Glock-Kuhn-Osthus survey treat only trees. A large-m proof may be an adaptation of the existing machinery, which caps the importance. The M was made precise and the rho-labelling strengthening added.

title: Two-frequency localization
W: Take a one-dimensional lattice Schrödinger operator whose potential is the sum of two cosines with frequencies √2 and √3, and make the coupling strong. Prove that for these specific frequencies, not just for almost every frequency pair, almost every phase gives localized eigenfunctions that decay exponentially.
M: For $\lambda>0$ and $\theta\in\mathbb T^2$ let $(H_{\lambda,\theta}\psi)(n)=\psi(n+1)+\psi(n-1)+\lambda\big(\cos2\pi(n\sqrt2+\theta_1)+\cos2\pi(n\sqrt3+\theta_2)\big)\psi(n)$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb Z)$. Prove there is $\lambda_0$ such that for all $\lambda\ge\lambda_0$ and Lebesgue-a.e. $\theta$, $H_{\lambda,\theta}$ has pure point spectrum with exponentially decaying eigenfunctions (Anderson localization).
why: Multi-frequency localization at large coupling is known only for a full-measure set of frequency vectors, because the proofs (Bourgain-Goldstein, Bourgain-Goldstein-Schlag) delete frequencies by semi-algebraic elimination. Proving it for one explicit Diophantine vector such as (√2,√3), which is Diophantine by Schmidt's subspace theorem, would require an arithmetic way to control double resonances, as Jitomirskaya's method does for one frequency.
issues: This is a special case of a recognised open problem (fixed-frequency localization for multi-frequency analytic potentials), not a new question. arXiv 2603.07180 says it is unknown whether some Diophantine frequency can be fixed, and solves only the dual perturbative regime on Z^d. Eliasson (Acta Math 1997) gives pure point spectrum at fixed Diophantine frequency for large Gevrey/analytic couplings, but without exponential decay of eigenfunctions, so the exponential decay is the open content. The original fixed coupling 10 was arbitrary: every known method gives an inexplicit lambda_0, so I replaced it with 'all lambda >= lambda_0'.

title: Rupert superballs
W: A cube can pass through a hole drilled in a copy of itself; a round ball cannot. Show that every superball between them, |x|^p+|y|^p+|z|^p ≤ 1 with p > 2, can.
M: Let $B_p=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x_1|^p+|x_2|^p+|x_3|^p\le1\}$ and $q=p/(p-1)$. Prove that for every $p\in(2,\infty)$ there are orthogonal projections $\pi_1,\pi_2$ of $\mathbb R^3$ onto planes and a rigid motion $\rho$ with $\rho(\pi_1(B_p))\subset\operatorname{int}\pi_2(B_p)$. By central symmetry this is equivalent to: there are orthonormal pairs $(a_1,a_2),(b_1,b_2)$ in $\mathbb R^3$ with $\|\cos t\,b_1+\sin t\,b_2\|_q>\|\cos t\,a_1+\sin t\,a_2\|_q$ for all $t$.
why: The Rupert property has been settled for many polyhedra, and a convex polyhedron without it was found in 2025. Smooth, strictly convex bodies are much less studied. The superball family interpolates between the Rupert cube and the non-Rupert ball, so it asks whether any loss of roundness at all creates a passage.
issues: Numerically this looks true and fairly routine. Central symmetry reduces it to comparing q-norms on two planes, with zero translation. Optimisation found positive margins of about 0.0018, 0.007, 0.027, 0.063 and 0.076 at p = 2.05, 2.2, 3, 10 and 60, with the margin growing roughly like 0.035(p-2) near p=2. A proof likely combines first-order perturbation at p=2 (an explicit configuration with positive linearised margin), continuity to the Rupert cube as p→∞, and interval arithmetic in between. That makes it computer-assisted routine work rather than a deep problem. The literature search found no prior treatment of superballs.

title: Minimal-mass blow-up with reflection
W: Consider the 2D Schrödinger equation in which the self-interaction at each point uses the density at the mirror point -x. Below the ground-state mass, solutions exist forever. Show that the only solutions that blow up with exactly the ground-state mass are the explicit pseudo-conformal ground-state solutions centred at the origin.
M: Let $Q>0$ be the radial solution of $\Delta Q-Q+Q^3=0$ on $\mathbb R^2$. Consider $iu_t+\Delta u+|u(-x,t)|^2u=0$ with $u_0\in H^1(\mathbb R^2)$ and $\|u_0\|_{L^2}=\|Q\|_{L^2}$. Prove that if $u$ blows up at a finite time $T$, then there are $\theta\in\mathbb R$ and $\lambda>0$ with $u(t,x)=e^{i\theta}\frac{\lambda}{T-t}\,Q\!\Big(\frac{\lambda x}{T-t}\Big)\exp\!\Big(i\frac{\lambda^2}{T-t}-i\frac{|x|^2}{4(T-t)}\Big)$.
why: Merle's classification of minimal-mass blow-up for the focusing mass-critical NLS is a model rigidity theorem. The reflection nonlinearity breaks translation and Galilean invariance but keeps scaling and the pseudo-conformal symmetry about the origin. It is therefore a simple test of which symmetries the rigidity argument actually needs.
issues: This looks like a routine adaptation of Merle (1993). The equation is Hamiltonian with $E=\int|\nabla u|^2-\tfrac12\int|u(x)|^2|u(-x)|^2$, and Cauchy-Schwarz gives $\int|u|^2|u(-\cdot)|^2\le\|u\|_4^4$. So the sharp threshold is $\|Q\|_2$, and equality forces $|u(x)|=|u(-x)|$, which puts the concentration point at the origin. The key estimate $E(e^{is\varphi}u)\ge0$ still holds because the nonlinearity depends only on $|u|$. The variance identity $V''=16E$ survives, and fewer symmetries means fewer parameters. I found no paper on this exact nonlinearity; the AKNS-type PT/reverse-space NLS literature treats $u^2\bar u(-x)$ instead. I made the M explicit: blow-up time T, phase and scale as the only free parameters.

W: Two identical point vortices moving on the surface of a cube form a two-degree-of-freedom Hamiltonian system with no continuous symmetry, so there is no second conserved quantity to make it integrable. Prove their motion is genuinely chaotic.
M:
Let $S$ be the boundary of the unit cube with its flat cone metric (eight cone points $v_i$ of angle $3\pi/2$), area $A=6$. Let $G$ solve $-\Delta_zG(z,w)=\delta_w-1/A$ with $\int_SG(\cdot,w)\,dA=0$, and let $R(z)=\lim_{w	o z} ig[G(z,w)+	frac1{2\pi}\log d(z,w) ig]$ for $z

otin\{v_i\}\}$ with $\omega=dA(z_1)+dA(z_2)$, let $H=G(z_1,z_2)+	frac12(R(z_1)+R(z_2))$. Prove that the Hamiltonian flow has a compact invariant set, inside one energy level, on which its topological entropy is positive.
